The rules are the ones given for Python in [Local packages (`local-deps`)](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/languages/python.md#local-deps): only the top-level module may declare `local-deps`, and the path must be relative and stay inside the project (an in-project symlink reaches a crate kept elsewhere). The `editable` flag has no meaning for a crate, which is recompiled on every build anyway.

One limit is specific to Rust. A Morloc `record` cannot be bound to a struct defined in the crate, because the marshalling code Morloc generates for a record must be an `impl` in the pool crate, and Rust’s orphan rule forbids implementing a foreign trait for a foreign type. Share functions across the crate boundary, pass primitives, lists, tuples and strings, and assemble records on the Morloc side; a crate struct that must cross the boundary goes through a tuple in the bridge file.

## 9.5.4. One resolution per environment

Every pool starts from one `Cargo.lock`: the lock persisted with the runtime at `$MORLOC_HOME/rust/Cargo.lock`, extended by every crate a pool in this environment has resolved before (kept at `$MORLOC_STATE/cache/rust-env.v2.lock`). A pool whose crates are all pinned there is built `--offline`; cargo never consults the registry and every pool links the same compiled dependencies. A pool that declares a crate not yet in the lock resolves it once, over the network, and its pins are merged back, so the next pool needing that crate — in any program — builds offline too. A crate that needs a newer version of one the runtime pins (an `arrow-row` newer than the runtime’s `arrow-array`) is not merged back, so it resolves over the network on each build. Deleting `rust-env.v2.lock` costs one online resolution per external crate and nothing else.

The pool’s release profile is set by the `rust:lto` and `rust:opt-level` build parameters ([Build parameters](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/languages/build-parameters.md)); `rust:lto` is the one setting that trades link time against cross-crate optimization.


---

<!-- https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/languages/futhark.html -->

# 9.6. Futhark

Morloc Manual > Language Support | https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/languages/futhark.html | prev: https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/languages/rust.md | next: https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/utilities/index.md

## 9.6.1. Futhark backends and GPU devices

Futhark code is compiled for a backend chosen with two build parameters ([Build parameters](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/languages/build-parameters.md)):

-   `backend` — the Futhark compilation backend: one of `c` (the default, sequential CPU), `multicore` (parallel CPU), `opencl`, `cuda`, `hip`, or `ispc`. The GPU backends (`opencl`, `cuda`, `hip`) are what make Futhark run on a GPU.
-   `device` — which device to run on, for a GPU backend, using Futhark’s device selector syntax (`#0`, `#1`, …​). It is only valid together with a GPU backend.

```bash
# build the Futhark kernels for CUDA and run on the second GPU
morloc make -X futhark:backend=cuda -X futhark:device=#1 -o nexus main.loc
```

A GPU build runs on the single selected device, and calls into the Futhark context are serialized. The required GPU runtime libraries (for example `-lcuda -lnvrtc` for CUDA) are linked automatically; if your toolchain lives in a non-standard location, add the paths with the C++ escape hatch, e.g. `-X cpp:flags=-L/usr/local/cuda/lib64`.


---

<!-- https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/utilities/ -->

# 10. Utilities

Morloc Manual | https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/utilities/ | prev: https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/languages/futhark.md | next: https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/utilities/nexus-file.md

The nexus has two subcommands that work on data files without a compiled Morloc program: `file` identifies a file, and `view` loads it and re-emits it in a chosen format. Call them on `morloc-nexus` directly; they take no manifest, so no program launcher is involved.

To inspect a binary result:

```console
$ ./myprog -f packet -o result.packet mycmd
$ morloc-nexus file result.packet
$ morloc-nexus view result.packet -f json | jq '.' | less
```


---

<!-- https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/utilities/nexus-file.html -->

# 10.1. morloc-nexus file

Morloc Manual > Utilities | https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/utilities/nexus-file.html | prev: https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/utilities/index.md | next: https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/utilities/nexus-view.md

`morloc-nexus file` plays the role of the UNIX `file` utility for Morloc-compatible data files. It recognises morloc packets (`data-packet`, `call-packet`, `stream-packet`, `ping-packet`), JSON, MessagePack, CSV, Arrow IPC, Parquet, ASCII / UTF-8 text, and empty files.

Default output is exactly one line per input file, formatted as `<path>: <type> key=value ...`. The stream is grep / awk / sort friendly: `morloc-nexus file * | wc -l` always equals the number of input files.

For example:

```console
$ morloc-nexus file data.packet log.stream data.json data.mpk people.csv README empty.bin
data.packet: data-packet source=mesg format=msgpack schema="as" payload=1024 metadata=64 total=1120
log.stream: stream-packet schema="ad8" state=final status=closed subpackets=42 elements=524288 payload_full_size=8388608 payload_wire_size=524288
data.json: json
data.mpk: msgpack
people.csv: csv columns=3 delimiter=","
README: text encoding=ascii
empty.bin: empty
```

For morloc packets, classification is magic-byte based and seek-only, so even a multi-gigabyte CALL or STREAM packet costs a few hundred bytes of I/O. The on-disk file size is checked against the size declared in the packet header by default; truncated or oversize packets are reported and exit non-zero.

## 10.1.1. Stream packets

Stream-packet output carries the footer’s summary when one is present. `state=final` marks a cleanly closed stream (final footer + end-of-file tail present); `state=temp` marks an intermediate mid-stream footer written by an in-progress `@close`; `state=missing` marks a stream whose writer exited before writing a footer.

For `state=missing` files, `morloc-nexus file` runs a bounded forward scan of the sub-packet headers to report a best-effort `subpackets=N` and `elements=N` count. The scan is capped at 10 000 sub-packets (`MORLOC_FILE_MAX_SCAN_SUBPACKETS` to override); when the cap is hit the counts carry a trailing `+` and the file is flagged as truncated at the scan boundary. Scan results annotate the `state=missing` line but are diagnostic only: the file is left untouched. `morloc-nexus view` reuses the same scan to open the file through `IStream` or the pattern walker.

For the remaining formats, classification reads up to one kilobyte of the file and feeds it through the same parsers the runtime uses on real ingest.

## 10.1.2. Options

| `-F`, `--no-file` | Suppress the `<path>:` prefix. |
| --- | --- |
| `-D`, `--no-description` | Suppress every `key=value` field; keep only the type token. `-FD` combined yields a clean type stream for programmatic use. |
| `-v`, `--verbose` | Break the one-line rule. CALL packets emit one indented `arg[i]: data-packet ...` line per argument. CSV files emit one indented `<name>:<type>` line per column, with type inferred as one of `int`, `float`, `str`, `bool`, `date`, `time`, or `other`. STREAM packets emit the extended footer diag (writer pid, flush timestamps, oversize count, largest sub-packet, EOF tail window). |
| `-n`, `--bytes SIZE` | Bytes read for content-based detection. Accepts a K / M / G suffix. Default `1k`. Morloc-packet detection always uses only the 32-byte header. |
| `--json` | Emit one JSON object per file. JSON output is unaffected by `-F` / `-D` / `-v` and always includes the full structure, including CSV column names and types. |
| `--validate` | After classifying, fully load each file through the exact same loader the `run` subcommand uses, then discard the result. Appends `validated=yes`, `validated=no error="<msg>"`, or `validated=structure-only`. If `file --validate` passes, `run` (or `view`) reading the same file will not fail at the load stage. |
| `--schema STRING` | Morloc schema used by `--validate` for inputs that don’t embed one. Ignored without `--validate`. |

## 10.1.3. Verbose example

```console
$ morloc-nexus file -v people.csv
people.csv: csv columns=3 delimiter=","
  name:str
  age:int
  city:str

$ morloc-nexus file -v call.packet
call.packet: call-packet midx=42 entrypoint=local nargs=3 payload=72 total=104
  arg[0]: data-packet source=mesg format=msgpack schema="i4" payload=4
  arg[1]: data-packet source=mesg format=msgpack schema="as" payload=16
  arg[2]: data-packet source=rptr format=voidstar schema="ad8" payload=8

$ morloc-nexus file -v log.stream
log.stream: stream-packet schema="ad8" state=final status=closed subpackets=42 elements=524288 payload_full_size=8388608 payload_wire_size=524288
  diag_version=1
  writer_pid=12345
  n_oversize_subpackets=0
  writer_start_time=1720000000
  first_flush_time=1720000001
  last_flush_time=1720000042
  largest_packet_uncompressed=262144
  largest_packet_idx=17
  tail_window=[...]
```


---

<!-- https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/utilities/nexus-view.html -->

# 10.2. morloc-nexus view

Morloc Manual > Utilities | https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/utilities/nexus-view.html | prev: https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/utilities/nexus-file.md | next: https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/ecosystem-architecture/index.md

Reads a data file (morloc data-packet, morloc stream-packet, `.json`, `.mpk`, `.arrow`, `.parquet`, or `.csv`) and re-emits it in a chosen output format. The intended use is ad-hoc inspection (`view foo.packet | jq | less`), one-shot format conversion (`view foo.json -f mpk --schema "as" -o foo.mpk`), and slicing large files down to a subset without materialising the whole thing (`view foo.packet --pattern ".[100:200]" -f json`).

`view` reuses the same loader chain `run` uses for argument ingress and the same output emitter `run` uses for results, so format support and conversion behaviour cannot drift away from a real morloc program run. A file accepted by `view` is one `run` would also accept, and vice versa.

```console
$ ./myprog -f packet -o result.packet mycmd
$ morloc-nexus view result.packet -f json
[1,2,3]
$ morloc-nexus view result.packet -f json | jq '. | length'
3
$ morloc-nexus view data.json -f mpk --schema "as" -o data.mpk
```

Before loading, `view` runs the same classifier `morloc-nexus file` uses, so a truncated or oversize morloc packet is rejected up-front with a clear error instead of decoding garbage from a partial payload.

## 10.2.1. Reading from stdin

A single `-` argument reads from stdin. For stream-packet input (the IFile / OStream / IStream shape), `view -` iterates sub-packet by sub-packet and emits one element (or one line, for `-f jsonl`) at a time, so a multi-gigabyte stream can be viewed in constant memory. For data-packet input, or when the selected output form requires a full-value load (e.g. `-f arrow`), stdin is drained to a `$TMPDIR` temp file and the normal file path runs. The temp file is deleted on exit.

```console
$ ./producer | morloc-nexus view - -f jsonl | head -5
```

## 10.2.2. Schema resolution

`view` always loads through the typed loader, so a schema is required:

1.  `--schema STRING` if given.
2.  Otherwise, the schema embedded in a morloc-packet’s metadata (data or stream).
3.  Otherwise, `view` exits with an error directing the user to `--schema`.

## 10.2.3. `--pattern`: extract a subset

`--pattern STR` applies a morloc pattern chain to the input before emission. The grammar is the same one morloc source uses for bracket accessors: field access (`.foo`), tuple/positional index (`.0`, `.1`), bracket index and slice (`.[i]`, `.[a:b]`, `.[a:b:c]`), grouped projection (`.(.a;.b)`), and broadcast tails after a slice (`.[:].name`, `.[:].[0]`, `.[:].(.name;.age)`).

The pattern is parsed and type-checked against the input’s schema before any I/O happens. Mismatches (a `.foo` on an integer, a slice on a scalar) fail with a diagnostic that points at the offending pattern fragment.

The group separator may be `;` (`.(.a;.b)`) or `,` as in Morloc source (`.(.a,.b)`); both mean the same thing.

```console
$ morloc-nexus view people.packet --pattern ".[0:10].(.name;.age)" -f json
[["Alice",30],["Bob",25],...]

$ morloc-nexus view timeseries.stream --pattern ".[100000:100010]" -f jsonl
{"t":1.0,"v":3.14}
{"t":1.01,"v":3.15}
...
```

The pattern dispatches through the same IFile walker `IFile a` values use in morloc code (`mlc_ifile_walk`) — for a data packet, a single mmap + slice; for a stream packet with a valid footer, `log2(K)` seeks over `K` sub-packets. For footer-less streams, `view` forward-scans the file to reconstruct the sub-packet index before dispatch (see [Footer-less streams](#footer-less-streams) below).

## 10.2.4. Packet-shape output: `-s` / `-d` / `-p`

Three mutually exclusive flags control the packet shape when the output form is a morloc packet:

| `-s`, `--stream-packet` | Emit a `MORLOC_STREAM_PACKET` file. The value (or the pattern result) must be a list. Implies `-f packet`. |
| --- | --- |
| `-d`, `--data-packet` | Emit a `MORLOC_DATA_PACKET` file (the default packet shape). Implies `-f packet`. |
| `-p`, `--preserve-packet` | Mirror the input packet’s shape on output: data-in / data-out, stream-in / stream-out. Errors when the input is not a morloc packet. Implies `-f packet`. |

Bare `-f packet` (no `-s`/`-d`/`-p`) emits a data packet. Any of `-s`/`-d`/`-p` combined with `-f <not packet>` is an error.

The four conversion arms all preserve typed semantics through the runtime’s authoritative packet writers:

-   **DATA → DATA** is a byte-level copy (or a loader re-emit when the `--schema` differs from the one embedded in the input).
-   **DATA → STREAM** opens the input as an IFile, chunks the array via bracket-slice, and writes each chunk through an OStream so the output is chunked, compressed, and indexed like any other stream file.
-   **STREAM → STREAM** drains the input via IStream `@next` and rewrites via OStream `@write`, so recompression, schema override, and footer normalisation all flow through the canonical writers. When `--compression-level` matches the source, a fast path verbatim-copies sub-packet payloads and only rewrites the footer.
-   **STREAM → DATA** materialises the whole stream to memory via the IFile walker and re-emits as a data packet. Gated by the size guardrail below.

## 10.2.5. `-f jsonl`: line-delimited JSON

`jsonl` output emits one JSON value per input element, one per line. JSON emission is element-by-element in all cases, so peak per-line memory is one element’s JSON body regardless of input size. Input buffering depends on the source:

-   stdin (`view - -f jsonl`) reads one sub-packet at a time and serialises its elements before reading the next, so a multi-GB producer streams through in constant memory.
-   File-based stream input goes through the buffered loader: the whole list is materialised, then emitted line-by-line. Combine with `--pattern .[a:b]` (or `-f jsonl` on stdin) for a constant-memory shape on multi-GB inputs.

## 10.2.6. Size guardrails and `--force`

Two guardrails refuse large operations without an explicit `--force`:

-   Any buffered path (stream input to a non-`jsonl` text output, stream input to a data packet, single-value binary output) whose projected working set exceeds 1 GiB.
-   Binary output (`-f packet`, `-f mpk`, `-f voidstar`, `-f arrow`, `-f parquet`) to a terminal.

`--force` lifts both. Refusal messages state which guardrail fired and suggest an alternative (`-s`, `-f jsonl`, `--pattern ".[a:b]"`, or `-o FILE`). The buffered-path threshold can be overridden with `MORLOC_VIEW_MAX_BUFFER_BYTES`.

For footer-less stream input the projected size falls back to the compressed file’s on-disk length as a conservative lower bound, so a partially-written multi-GB stream still hits the guardrail rather than silently OOM’ing the buffered path.

## 10.2.7. Footer-less streams

A stream file whose final footer is missing (writer crashed before `@close`, `program > out.stream` interrupted, etc.) is still usable through `view`. The classifier reports the missing footer, and:

-   `view -p` (or explicit `-s`) re-emits a well-formed stream with a canonical footer — the runtime’s IStream drains forward regardless of footer state, and OStream writes a fresh footer.
-   `view -d` (buffered materialisation) succeeds subject to the size guardrail.
-   `view --pattern PATTERN` forward-scans the file to recover a sub-packet-offset index, then dispatches the walker as normal.

## 10.2.8. Options

| `-f`, `--output-form FORM` | Output format: `json` (default), `jsonl`, `mpk`, `voidstar`, `packet`, `arrow`, `parquet`, `csv`. Same set as `run -f` plus `jsonl`. |
| --- | --- |
| `-z`, `--compression-level N` | zstd preset `0..=9`. Applies to each sub-packet when emitting `-s` (stream packet). |
| `-o`, `--output-file PATH` | Write to `PATH` instead of stdout. |
| `-s`, `--stream-packet` | Emit a stream packet (mutex with `-d`/`-p`). |
| `-d`, `--data-packet` | Emit a data packet (mutex with `-s`/`-p`). |
| `-p`, `--preserve-packet` | Mirror the input packet’s shape (mutex with `-s`/`-d`). |
| `--pattern STR` | Apply a pattern chain (`.[a:b].field`, `.[:].[0]`, …​) before emission. |
| `--force` | Lift the size and binary-to-tty guardrails. |
| `--schema STRING` | Morloc schema string (compact format, e.g. `"as"` for `[Str]`, `"ad8"` for `[F64]`). Overrides the input’s embedded schema. |


---

<!-- https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/ecosystem-architecture/ -->

# 11. Ecosystem Architecture

Morloc Manual | https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/ecosystem-architecture/ | prev: https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/utilities/nexus-view.md | next: https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/ecosystem-architecture/eco-overview.md

This chapter specifies how the parts of the Morloc ecosystem fit together: the compiler, the runtime library, the nexus, and the environment manager `mim`. It defines where each part is installed, how the runtime is built, how an `import` finds a module, how a program’s foreign packages are solved into an environment, how a compiled program is served to other programs and agents, and how an environment is frozen into a portable image. The [Deployment](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/apis/index.md) chapter shows how to use these tools; this chapter specifies what they do.

This chapter and the two that follow are written as a specification. They describe behavior, formats and guarantees rather than any particular implementation, so they should remain true of any conforming reimplementation.


---

<!-- https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/ecosystem-architecture/eco-overview.html -->

# 11.1. Overview

Morloc Manual > Ecosystem Architecture | https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/ecosystem-architecture/eco-overview.html | prev: https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/ecosystem-architecture/index.md | next: https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/ecosystem-architecture/eco-environments.md

> The Morloc ecosystem has four parts. The **compiler** turns Morloc source into a build directory. The **runtime library** is linked into every pool and implements the shared formats. The **nexus** runs a compiled program, from the command line or as a server. The **environment manager**, `mim`, creates isolated installations of the other three, solves the foreign packages that programs need, and serves and freezes the result. This section says what each part owns, when each runs, where an installation keeps its files, and how the parts agree on versions.

**Who invokes whom.**

| Stage | What runs | What it produces |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Provision | `mim` downloads a compiler release and builds an environment; inside it, `morloc init` builds the runtime ([Runtime bootstrap](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/ecosystem-architecture/eco-bootstrap.md)) | An installation |
| Install | `morloc install` fetches modules ([Module resolution](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/ecosystem-architecture/eco-modules.md)) | Module source in the installation |
| Build | `morloc make`, which calls back into `mim` to solve packages ([Environment solving](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/ecosystem-architecture/eco-solving.md)) | A build directory and launchers ([Compilation artifacts](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-artifacts.md)) |
| Run | A launcher runs the nexus, which starts the pools ([Runtime overview](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-overview.md)) | A result |
| Serve | The nexus as a server, started by `mim` ([Serving](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/ecosystem-architecture/eco-serving.md)) | MCP tools and HTTP endpoints |
| Freeze | `mim` builds an image of the environment ([Freezing](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/ecosystem-architecture/eco-freezing.md)) | A container image |

The compiler and `mim` are coupled only across process boundaries: files the compiler writes, commands it runs, and environment variables. In every such contract the compiler (or its release) writes and `mim` reads, so the burden of compatibility falls on `mim`.

**An installation** is two directory trees. The **home** holds what `morloc init` builds and is the same for every program; the **state** holds what accumulates as modules and programs are installed. They are the same directory unless the state is given its own location.

```
<home>/
|-- bin/           morloc-nexus, and the launcher of each installed program
|-- lib/           the runtime library and per-language libraries
|-- include/       the runtime's C header and per-language headers
|-- opt/           per-language setup state
`-- rust/          the runtime's source, kept for building Rust pools

<state>/
|-- src/morloc/plane/<plane>/<module>/   installed module source
|-- fdb/           one record per installed module, and install locks
|-- modules/       files that modules expose to foreign code
|-- exe/<program>/ installed programs: source copy and build directory
`-- snapshots/     module version pins
```

The home defaults to `~/.local/share/morloc`. Inside an environment, `mim` gives each environment its own home and state, so nothing is shared between environments except downloads ([Environments](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/ecosystem-architecture/eco-environments.md)).

**Version agreement.** Three rules keep the parts consistent:

-   **Compiler and nexus.** A build’s manifest records the compiler’s version. The nexus runs a manifest only if it was written by the same Morloc version ([Compilation artifacts](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-artifacts.md)).
-   **Compiler and runtime.** The runtime is built from the source shipped with the compiler’s own release, by that compiler, so they agree by construction. The runtime library also declares a numeric ABI version, which the nexus reports.
-   **Compiler and `mim`.** Each document the compiler hands to `mim` carries its own version: the dependency specification an integer, the language-support table a `MAJOR.MINOR` schema. A release lists these versions in its manifest so that `mim` can refuse, before installing anything, a release it cannot read ([Runtime bootstrap](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/ecosystem-architecture/eco-bootstrap.md)).


---

<!-- https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/ecosystem-architecture/eco-environments.html -->

# 11.2. Environments

Morloc Manual > Ecosystem Architecture | https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/ecosystem-architecture/eco-environments.html | prev: https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/ecosystem-architecture/eco-overview.md | next: https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/ecosystem-architecture/eco-bootstrap.md

> An **environment** is one complete Morloc installation managed by `mim`: a compiler, its runtime, a solved set of language toolchains and packages, and the programs installed into it. Every other `mim` operation acts on one environment. This section specifies an environment’s identity, where its files live, how commands run inside it, and what holds when it is changed or removed.

**Identity.** An environment is a name within a **scope**. The **local** scope belongs to one user and needs no privileges; the **system** scope is shared by every user on the machine, and only root may create, change, serve or remove its environments (any user may run commands in one). A name is 1 to 64 characters of ASCII letters, digits, `-`, `_` and `.`, beginning with a letter or digit, unique within its scope. A lookup by name tries the local scope first, so a local environment may shadow a system one of the same name.

**Backend.** Each environment has one backend, fixed at creation:

| Backend | How commands run |
| --- | --- |
| Native | On the host, against a toolchain installed in the environment’s own directory. |
| Container | In a container started from the environment’s own image, by Docker, Podman or Apptainer. |

When no backend is named, `mim` chooses native where the host can run it (glibc Linux, Apple Silicon macOS, or NixOS with `nix` and unprivileged user namespaces), and otherwise a configured container engine or the only one installed. With several engines and no configured choice it asks rather than guessing.

**Files.** Each scope has a configuration root and a data root:

| Scope | Configuration | Data |
| --- | --- | --- |
| local | `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/morloc` (default `~/.config/morloc`) | `$XDG_DATA_HOME/morloc` (default `~/.local/share/morloc`) |
| system | `/etc/morloc` | `/usr/local/share/morloc` |

An environment’s configuration directory holds its settings, its views ([Serving](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/ecosystem-architecture/eco-serving.md)), its extra engine flags and the record of its running server. It is small, edited by `mim` only, and never visible inside the environment. The environment exists exactly when its settings record does.

Its data directory holds everything the environment’s programs see: the Morloc home and state ([Overview](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/ecosystem-architecture/eco-overview.md)), the solved toolchain and its lock, the recorded requirements of every program ([Environment solving](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/ecosystem-architecture/eco-solving.md)), the home directory of its shell, and its server logs. Downloads that environments can share — compiler releases, the solver binary, `mim` binaries for other platforms — are stored once per scope in the data root and never modified after they are complete.

**The default environment.** A command that names no environment acts on the default. Each scope records at most one default, by name. The local default wins if it names an existing environment; otherwise the system default applies. There is no activation step and no variable that selects an environment, so a command means the same thing in every shell.

**Running a command.** `mim run` and `mim shell` execute a command with the environment’s compiler, runtime, toolchain and installed programs first on the `PATH` and its home as `MORLOC_HOME`. The working directory is the user’s current directory, mounted at `/work` in a container, and files written there belong to the invoking user. A container sees only the host variables passed to it explicitly. The command’s exit status becomes \`mim’s.

Three variables mark a command as running in a managed environment, and are set together:

| Variable | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `MORLOC_ENV` | Non-empty inside a managed environment. `morloc make` solves packages only when it is set. |
| `MORLOC_BUILD_HOOK` | The program `morloc make` calls to solve packages: the `mim` that manages this environment. |
| `MORLOC_BIN` | The compiler, so the hook asks the exact compiler that is building for its language requirements. |

The hook is `mim` itself, in the same binary as the manager. Staging the manager’s own binary into the environment keeps the two at one version.

Before a solve, a build or a native command, `mim` removes the variables of any other conda, mamba or pixi environment active in the user’s shell. Their activation scripts add compiler flags and library paths, and mixing two package worlds produces binaries that link against both.

**Changing an environment.** `mim update` rebuilds an environment and `mim modify` changes its settings, rebuilding when the toolchain changes. The Morloc version an environment was provisioned with moves only when an update asks for another version explicitly; no other command changes it. A move is refused if an installed module declares a range of Morloc versions that excludes the target. A change either completes or leaves the environment’s settings, requirements and solved toolchain as they were.

**Removal.** `mim rm` stops the environment’s server, then removes its configuration, data, image and volumes. It leaves alone directories the user supplied (a host directory mounted as its home) and the shared downloads, so a later `mim new` does not start from nothing.


---

<!-- https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/ecosystem-architecture/eco-bootstrap.html -->

# 11.3. Runtime bootstrap

Morloc Manual > Ecosystem Architecture | https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/ecosystem-architecture/eco-bootstrap.html | prev: https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/ecosystem-architecture/eco-environments.md | next: https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/ecosystem-architecture/eco-caching.md

> Before any program can be compiled, an installation needs a compiler and a runtime built for the machine it runs on. The compiler is distributed as a prebuilt binary in a release; the runtime is built from source on the target by `morloc init`, against the toolchain the environment provides. This section specifies what a release contains, how `mim` verifies and installs it, what `morloc init` produces, and when it rebuilds.

## 11.3.1. Releases

A release is named by a tag. `latest` means the newest release, and a bare version such as `0.105.2` means tag `v0.105.2`. Each release publishes a **release manifest**, a JSON object:

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `schema` | The manifest’s own format version. A reader refuses a schema newer than it knows. |
| `version` | The Morloc version the release contains. |
| `triples` | Per platform (`linux-x86_64`, `linux-arm64`, `macos-arm64`), the name of the compiler binary. |
| `rust_src` | The name of the archive holding the runtime’s source. |
| `sha256` | The SHA-256 digest of every asset. |
| `versions` | The contract versions of this release: `morloc_version`, `abi_version`, `envspec_version`, `lang_support_schema`. |

`mim` reads the manifest before downloading anything else and refuses a release whose contract versions it cannot read, telling the user to upgrade `mim`. A platform the manifest does not list is refused with a pointer to a container backend, since a container runs the Linux build on any host.

Every asset is downloaded to a temporary name, checked against its digest, and only then renamed into place. A missing digest is a refusal, not a warning. A downloaded release is stored once per scope, keyed by version and platform, and marked complete only after all of its assets are in place; an incomplete one is never used.

## 11.3.2. Building an environment

For a container backend, `mim` first builds an image for the environment from a base Linux image, the system packages the user asked for, any extra certificate authorities, the compiler, the runtime source, and its own binary. It is rebuilt only when one of these inputs changes. The solved toolchain and the built runtime are not in the image: they live in the environment’s data and are mounted in, so a package change does not rebuild the image.

Then, for every backend, `mim` solves the toolchain the compiler requires ([Environment solving](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/ecosystem-architecture/eco-solving.md)) and runs `morloc init` inside the environment, in a strict mode in which every compiler and interpreter must come from the solved toolchain rather than the host.

An environment can carry a bundle of extra certificate authorities, for networks that inspect TLS. The bundle is checked to contain certificates only (a private key is refused), installed as a trusted root in the image, and passed to the solver and every package manager in the environment.

## 11.3.3. What `morloc init` produces

`morloc init` builds the runtime into the Morloc home:

| Output | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `include/morloc.h` | The runtime’s C API ([Runtime library API](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-libmorloc.md)). |
| `lib/` runtime library | The shared library every pool links against. |
| `bin/morloc-nexus` | The nexus. |
| Per-language bindings | One for each supported language whose tools are present: a Python extension module, an R library, a C++ library and precompiled header, a prebuilt Rust crate. |
| `rust/` | A copy of the runtime source, used when compiling Rust pools. |

The runtime source is found, in order, at a path named by `MORLOC_RUST_DIR`, in the home’s `rust/` directory, or beside the compiler binary. Building it requires a Rust toolchain. The runtime is always built optimized; a sanitizer variant exists for debugging the runtime itself.

A language whose tools are missing is skipped with a warning, and its programs cannot be built until a later `init` succeeds. In strict mode a missing or foreign tool is an error instead, so an environment never silently falls back to the host’s compiler.

Only one `init` runs per home at a time; a second waits for the first. `init` rebuilds the runtime and every language binding unless it is run in incremental mode, which keeps each part that is already present. `-f` also removes the files `init` owns before rebuilding, so a binding left by an older version cannot survive.

`init` links `morloc-nexus` into a directory on the user’s `PATH` (by default `~/.local/bin` when it exists; `MORLOC_BIN_LINK_DIR` names another, and an empty value turns linking off). `mim` turns it off inside environments so that no environment changes the user’s global commands.

**Interpreter pinning.** The Python and R bindings are compiled against one minor version of their interpreter. Once an environment has built them, the interpreter’s minor version is pinned in every later solve of that environment ([Environment solving](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/ecosystem-architecture/eco-solving.md)), and a binding that no longer matches its interpreter is rebuilt before the next build uses it.


---

<!-- https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/ecosystem-architecture/eco-caching.html -->

# 11.4. Caching

Morloc Manual > Ecosystem Architecture | https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/ecosystem-architecture/eco-caching.html | prev: https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/ecosystem-architecture/eco-bootstrap.md | next: https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/ecosystem-architecture/eco-remote.md

> A label that asks for `cache` makes each call through it look up its result on disk before computing it, and store the result after. The cache is shared by every program, pool language and run on a machine, and by every machine that mounts the same directory. This section specifies what identifies a call, where entries live, how they are written so that readers never see a partial one, and what invalidates them. What a label wraps, and when a cached call is worth making, is in [Caching](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/runs/caching.md).

**What is cached.** A label wraps one call of a function, or one run of a suspension. A cached call is looked up when it is made and stored when it returns. A call that fails is not stored, so the same call fails again rather than returning a value that was never computed. A suspension is cached per run: a held suspension run twice looks up twice, and the second run is a hit. Caching is the user’s claim that the call returns the same value whenever it is made with the same inputs; the runtime does not check it.

**The key.** A call is identified by three things, hashed with XXH64 into a 64-bit key:

-   The **fingerprint** of the pool the call runs in. A pool is the process that runs one language’s share of a program. Its fingerprint covers the pool’s generated source, the contents of every file the program lists under `hash-include`, the build parameters, and any compiled guest objects linked into it. The compiler computes it once per build and records it in the manifest; the nexus hands it to the pool.
-   The **call site**: the compiler’s identifier for the labeled call within the build.
-   The **value** of each argument, or for a suspension, of each value it captured. A value is hashed by walking it as its type describes it, so the hash does not depend on where the value is stored (inline in a message, in shared memory, or in a file) and never covers a pointer.

The arguments are evaluated by the caller before the lookup, so evaluating them is never skipped by a hit. Anything that changes the pool’s generated source (editing Morloc code that compiles into the pool, or a build parameter) or a `hash-include` file changes the fingerprint, and every key from that pool with it. A sourced foreign file is covered only through the generated code that names it, so editing its contents changes nothing unless it is listed under `hash-include`. Nothing else does: the cache has no notion of time, and moving or copying a program does not invalidate it.

**Where entries live.** The cache base is the first of these that is set: `MORLOC_CACHE_BASE`; `$XDG_CACHE_HOME/morloc/cache`; `~/.cache/morloc/cache`; a `cache` directory in the user’s private runtime directory. An entry is two files under it:

```
<cache base>/
|-- <label>/<key>.dat     index: names the content file, and the value's type
`-- data/<hash>.dat       content: the value, as a self-contained data packet
```

The content file is named by the hash of the value it holds, so equal values stored by different labels, call sites or languages share one file. It is a data packet ([Packet protocol](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-packets.md)) whose payload holds the whole value, with every reference to a file handle replaced by the file’s path; it may be compressed at the level `MORLOC_CACHE_COMPRESSION_LEVEL` gives (default: none).

**Writing.** The cache takes no locks. Each file is written to a temporary name beside its target, synced, and renamed into place, so a reader sees the whole file or none of it. The content file is written first and skipped if it already exists; the index is written last. A crash between the two leaves an unreferenced content file, which a later store of the same value reuses. Concurrent stores of one key each write a complete file, and the last rename wins.

**Reading.** A lookup reads the index and follows it to the content. A missing index is a miss. So is an index that is too short to be a packet, that cannot be parsed, or whose content file is missing or empty; the lookup deletes it, and the call is computed and stored as if the entry had not existed.

Nothing is evicted: Morloc removes an entry only when a lookup finds it invalid. Deleting the cache base, or any part of it, is safe while no program is using it.


---

<!-- https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/ecosystem-architecture/eco-remote.html -->

# 11.5. Remote jobs

Morloc Manual > Ecosystem Architecture | https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/ecosystem-architecture/eco-remote.html | prev: https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/ecosystem-architecture/eco-caching.md | next: https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/ecosystem-architecture/eco-modules.md

> A label with a `remote:` block runs each call through it as a job on a SLURM cluster. The process that makes the call, the job’s **parent**, writes the call to a file, submits a job that runs the program’s nexus on that file, waits for the job to end, and reads its result back. This section specifies what the parent sends, the command the job runs, how the parent learns that the job has ended, the files the two share and how long they last, and the bridge through which a program in a container submits jobs to the host. What a label wraps is in [Remote job submission](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/runs/remote-jobs.md).

**When a call becomes a job.** Submission is compiled into a program only when its build asks for it, either for one build (`morloc make --slurm`) or for every build in an installation (`morloc init --slurm`). Otherwise a label’s `remote:` block is ignored and the call runs in the parent. A label wraps one call of a function, or one run of a suspension, and that call is the job’s work: the job runs the labeled function, and everything the function’s body calls. The parent evaluates the call’s arguments before it submits the job. A job’s parent may itself be a job.

When the label also asks for `cache`, the parent looks the call up in the cache ([Caching](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/ecosystem-architecture/eco-caching.md)) before submitting it; a hit submits nothing, and a result is stored only after the job has completed.

**What the parent sends.** The parent turns each argument into a self-contained data packet ([Packet protocol](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-packets.md)): the whole value is copied into the packet’s payload, so nothing in it refers to the parent’s shared memory. A file handle is sent as its path, which the job reopens. A value holding an input or output stream is refused, since a stream belongs to the process that opened it. The arguments go into one call packet, which names the call by the compiler’s identifier for it.

**The job’s directory.** Each call gets a new directory under the cache base, `<cache base>/_remote/<name>/`, where the name joins the parent’s host name, its process id, a counter and the time, and the directory is created exclusively, so no two calls share one. The cache base is resolved as in [Caching](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/ecosystem-architecture/eco-caching.md). The parent and the job must see it at the same path, so on a cluster it must be on a filesystem every node mounts.

| File | Contents |
| --- | --- |
| `call.dat` | The call packet, written by the parent before submission |
| `result.dat` | The result packet, written by the job |
| `job.out`, `job.err` | The job’s standard output and error, written by SLURM |

**Submission.** The parent submits with

```
sbatch --parsable -o <dir>/job.out -e <dir>/job.err [resources] --wrap='<command>'
```

and reads the job’s id from the output. The resources are the label’s: memory as `--mem=<N>G`, wall time as `--time=<D-HH:MM:SS>`, CPU cores as `--cpus-per-task=<N>`, and GPUs as `--gres=gpu:<N>`. A resource the label leaves unset is not requested, so the cluster’s default applies. Memory and time of 0 are requested as given, since SLURM gives them a meaning (all of a node’s memory, no limit); CPUs and GPUs of 0 are not requested, and in particular `--gres` is never passed without GPUs, since a cluster with no GPU resources defined rejects it.

The command runs the nexus of the parent’s own program, by absolute path, on the parent’s manifest:

```
<nexus> run --call-packet <dir>/call.dat --socket-base <pool socket name>
        --output-file <dir>/result.dat --output-form packet <manifest>
```

The job’s nexus sends the call to a pool of the labeled function’s language, started on the compute node, and writes the result as a self-contained packet to a temporary name beside `result.dat`, renamed into place when complete. SLURM starts a job in the directory `sbatch` ran in, which is the directory the parent was started from, and, by default, with the parent’s environment.

**Waiting.** The parent asks SLURM for the job’s state once a second, with

```
sacct -j <id> --format=State%30 --noheader
```

until a line names a state after which the job makes no further progress: `COMPLETED`, `FAILED`, `CANCELLED`, `TIMEOUT`, `OUT_OF_MEMORY`, `NODE_FAIL`, `BOOT_FAIL`, `DEADLINE` or `PREEMPTED`, including the forms SLURM abbreviates to its column width (`OUT_OF_ME+`) or annotates (`CANCELLED by 1234`).

**The result.** If the job ended `COMPLETED`, the parent reads `result.dat`, checks that it is a well-formed packet, refuses one holding an input stream, and returns it as the result of the labeled call. The parent then deletes the job’s directory, so a later identical call submits a new job.

A labeled function that fails in the job makes the job’s nexus write the error to its standard error and exit with a failure status, so the job ends `FAILED`. If the job ended in any state but `COMPLETED`, completed without writing a result, or wrote a malformed one, the call fails with an error naming the job, its state and the path of its standard error, followed by the first 4 KiB of that file; the directory is kept so the whole of it can be read. Nothing removes a failed job’s directory later.

**The bridge.** A program in a container has no `sbatch` or `sacct`. When `MORLOC_BRIDGE_SOCKET` names a Unix socket, the parent sends each submission and each status question to that socket instead, and `mim`, on the host, runs the SLURM commands. Each exchange is one connection carrying one JSON object on one line in each direction:

| Request | Fields | Reply |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `"op": "submit"` | `inner_argv` (the job’s command, one element per argument), `stdout`, `stderr`, `resources` (`mem_gb`, `time_s`, `cpus`, `gpus`) | `job_id`, or `error` |
| `"op": "status"` | `job_id` | `state` as SLURM names it, or `error` |

`mim` runs the command inside the same environment on the compute node, with the bridge enabled there too, so a job can submit jobs of its own. A status question that fails is treated as a job still running.


---

<!-- https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/ecosystem-architecture/eco-modules.html -->

# 11.6. Module resolution

Morloc Manual > Ecosystem Architecture | https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/ecosystem-architecture/eco-modules.html | prev: https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/ecosystem-architecture/eco-remote.md | next: https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/ecosystem-architecture/eco-solving.md

> A Morloc program is assembled from modules: its own source files and modules installed into the Morloc state. This section specifies how the compiler finds the file an `import` names, how a module is identified and installed, how versions are pinned, and how a module declares the foreign packages it needs. The install-string syntax is given in [Installing modules](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/modules/installing-modules.md).

## 11.6.1. Finding a module

An import names a module by dotted path. A leading dot makes it **local**: `import .foo.bar` is looked up only under the **project root**, the directory of the file being compiled, as `foo/bar.loc` and then `foo/bar/main.loc`. A program read from standard input has no project root and may not use local imports, and neither may an eval expression ([Serving](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/ecosystem-architecture/eco-serving.md)).

Without the leading dot the import is **bare**, and it names an installed module only. The search covers the installed modules of the active **plane** (a named namespace of installed modules; `default` unless configured), its core subdirectory (`morloclib`) first:

1.  `<plane>/morloclib/foo/bar/main.loc`
2.  `<plane>/morloclib/foo/bar.loc`
3.  `<plane>/foo/bar.loc`
4.  `<plane>/foo/bar/main.loc`
5.  the same two forms directly under the module tree, outside any plane

The first candidate that exists is taken; a local file of the same name is never used. A bare import that matches nothing is an error. When a local file of that name exists, the error names it and says to write `import .foo.bar`, and `morloc make` does not download a registry package of that name in its place. Otherwise the error lists every path tried and suggests `morloc install`.

A module named `owner/name` searches only the plane: `owner/name/main.loc`, `owner/name.loc`, then `name/main.loc` and `name.loc`.

The last three components of a matched path must have the exact spelling of the import, so a module resolves the same way on case-insensitive and case-sensitive file systems.

## 11.6.2. Identity

A module is a directory. Its entry file is `main.loc`, or its only `.loc` file. The entry file declares exactly one named module, and that name must equal the directory’s name (for an installed module, the repository’s name). A name is ASCII letters, digits and `-`, beginning with a letter or digit.

A module’s metadata is the `package.yaml` beside its entry file. The fields the ecosystem reads:

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `version` | The module’s own version. |
| `morloc-version` | The range of compiler versions the module accepts. A compiler outside it refuses to load the module. |
| `morloc-deps` | Pins for imported modules, each a name and a git hash. |
| `py-deps`, `r-deps`, `cpp-deps`, `rust-deps` | Foreign packages, each with a version constraint and a source ([Dependencies (`py-deps`)](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/languages/python.md#py-deps)). |
| `tool-deps` | conda packages whose executables the module runs as programs, whatever its languages ([Command-line tools (`tool-deps`)](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/apis/deploy-dependencies.md#tool-deps)). |
| `local-deps` | Packages kept inside the project tree ([Local packages (`local-deps`)](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/languages/python.md#local-deps)). Allowed only in the program being built, not in an imported module. |
| `lang-versions` | Constraints on the language runtimes themselves. |
| `dependencies` | System libraries. |
| `expose` | Files copied where foreign code can include or import them ([Exposing native resources](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/modules/exposing-native-resources.md)). |
| `setup` | A script run after the module is installed. |

## 11.6.3. Installing

`morloc install` fetches a module into `<plane>/<name>` in the Morloc state. Each install:

1.  takes a lock for that module name, so two installs of one module never interleave;
2.  fetches into a temporary directory beside the destination;
3.  checks that the module’s declared name matches and that its `morloc-version` admits this compiler;
4.  replaces the previous copy in one rename, so a failed install leaves the old one intact;
5.  installs every module it imports that is not already present, the same way;
6.  copies its `expose` files and runs its `setup` script, with the module’s name, version and directory in the environment;
7.  typechecks it, unless told not to;
8.  writes a record of the install: name, version, source and pinned hash.

A module that is already installed is left alone unless the install is forced. `morloc make` installs missing imports the same way before it compiles.

**Pins.** A pin fixes an imported module to a git hash. Pins come from the `morloc-deps` of the modules being installed (a pin closer to the program wins; two different pins at the same depth are an error) and from snapshot files in the state, which list `name hash` pairs for a whole installation. An installed module whose recorded hash differs from its pin is an error until it is reinstalled.

## 11.6.4. Foreign dependencies

The compiler gathers the foreign requirements of a program from every module it imports, transitively, and writes them beside the manifest as `envspec.json`. Constraints on one package from several modules are combined (all must hold), the C++ standard is the highest any module asks for, and two modules naming different conda channels for one package is an error, whether they request it as a language package or as a tool. The file also lists the program’s languages, the tools it runs (conda packages whose executables it calls, whatever its languages) and its system libraries. `morloc envspec` writes the same document without building. How the document is solved is specified in [Environment solving](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/ecosystem-architecture/eco-solving.md).


---

<!-- https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/ecosystem-architecture/eco-solving.html -->

# 11.7. Environment solving

Morloc Manual > Ecosystem Architecture | https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/ecosystem-architecture/eco-solving.html | prev: https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/ecosystem-architecture/eco-modules.md | next: https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/ecosystem-architecture/eco-serving.md

> A program’s foreign packages must be installed, at compatible versions, before its pools can compile or run. The compiler knows what a program needs; the environment manager knows how to provide it. This section specifies the contract between them: when the compiler asks, what it sends, how the manager turns every program’s requests into one solved set of packages, and what holds when solves fail or run at once.

## 11.7.1. The build hook

`morloc make` asks for its packages only inside a managed environment, when `MORLOC_ENV` is set ([Environments](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/ecosystem-architecture/eco-environments.md)). After writing the pool sources and before compiling them, it runs:

```
$MORLOC_BUILD_HOOK sync --name <key> --spec envspec.json --root <project> [--installed]
```

`<key>` is the program’s key ([Compilation artifacts](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-artifacts.md)), `envspec.json` is the document described in [Module resolution](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/ecosystem-architecture/eco-modules.md), and `--installed` marks a build that is being installed rather than built in place. The hook writes its messages to standard error. Exit status 0 means the environment now satisfies the specification; anything else fails the build. If `MORLOC_ENV` is set but no hook is named, a program that declares foreign packages fails to build, since nothing could provide them.

The hook asks the compiler named by `MORLOC_BIN` for its **language-support table**: for each language, the runtime package and version range the compiler supports and the packages its bindings need, plus the toolchain the compiler itself needs. A program’s request is always solved together with this table, so a program can never ask for an interpreter the runtime cannot bind.

Both documents carry versions. The dependency specification has an integer version that the reader must match exactly; it is refused with "rebuild the program" if older and "upgrade the manager" if newer. The language-support table has a `MAJOR.MINOR` schema; a reader accepts any minor version of the major it knows and ignores fields it does not recognise.

## 11.7.2. One world per environment

An environment has one set of installed packages, its **solved world**. It is the solution of the union of:

-   the specification of every installed program;
-   the specification of every program built in place (**scratch** builds), kept until the environment is cleaned;
-   the compiler’s language-support requirements;
-   extra packages the user named for the environment;
-   the interpreter pins (below).

One world means one version of each package. Two programs constraining the same package must both be satisfied. A requirement nobody can satisfy fails the command that added it.

Each requested package is provided, delegated or refused. conda and PyPI packages are solved into the world, and so are tools, the conda packages whose executables a program runs. Rust crates are left to cargo, which resolves them when the pool is compiled. A source the manager does not support is refused, never silently dropped, as are contradictory requests for one package: two conda channels, two local paths, or a local path and a version.

A local Python package of an installed program ([Local packages (`local-deps`)](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/languages/python.md#local-deps)) is copied into the environment under a name derived from a hash of its contents, and the requirement points at the copy. The installed program then no longer depends on the project directory, the same path is valid on the host, in a container and in a frozen image, and reinstalling unchanged source does no work. Copies that no installed program references are reclaimed.

## 11.7.3. Solving

Each environment has one solve lock, shared by the host and its container. Recording a program’s specification, gathering the world, solving it, and recording the result all happen while holding it, so concurrent builds in one environment serialize, and the second usually finds its world already solved.

The world reduces to a canonical **requirement digest**. If it equals the digest of the last successful solve and the solved packages are present, nothing is done. The digest is written last, after the packages are installed and their activation captured, so an interrupted solve is redone rather than trusted.

Otherwise the solver first tries to install the existing lock unchanged, and re-solves only if the lock cannot satisfy the new world. Package versions therefore move only when a new requirement forces them to.

**Interpreter pins.** The Python and R bindings are compiled against one minor version of their interpreter ([Runtime bootstrap](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/ecosystem-architecture/eco-bootstrap.md)). After the first solve that provides an interpreter, its minor version is pinned, and later solves stay within it. A requirement that needs another minor fails with a message to update the environment, which drops the pin and rebuilds the bindings.

**Failure.** If a solve fails, the requirements recorded for every program are restored to what they were before the command. The solver’s own manifest, lock and partially installed packages may be left changed; the next successful solve reconciles them, and the digest, removed at the start of the solve, guarantees that it runs.

**Immutable environments.** An environment marked immutable — one being served, or a frozen image — refuses any request that would change its world or rebuild a binding, before writing anything.

## 11.7.4. When solving happens

| Event | Solve |
| --- | --- |
| `morloc make` in an environment | Through the build hook, as above. |
| `mim install` | Once before the build, from the specification the compiler reports without building, so packages are present when the pools compile; then through the hook. |
| `mim modify` (languages, extra packages) and `mim update` | A solve of the whole world, followed by a rebuild of the runtime and bindings when the Morloc version or an interpreter changed. |
| Cleaning the environment | Scratch specifications are discarded and the world re-solved from installed programs only. |


---

<!-- https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/ecosystem-architecture/eco-serving.html -->

# 11.8. Serving

Morloc Manual > Ecosystem Architecture | https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/ecosystem-architecture/eco-serving.html | prev: https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/ecosystem-architecture/eco-solving.md | next: https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/ecosystem-architecture/eco-freezing.md

> A compiled program is a command-line tool, but the nexus can also keep it running as a server, answering many requests without restarting its pools. This section specifies the server modes, how one command of a manifest becomes an HTTP endpoint and an MCP tool, how a server recovers from a crashed pool, how callers may evaluate new expressions, and the security model that decides who may call what. How `mim` chooses what to serve is specified last.

## 11.8.1. Server modes

| Mode | Serves |
| --- | --- |
| Daemon | One program, to local clients over a Unix socket or loopback TCP (length-prefixed JSON), and optionally over HTTP. Starts every pool at startup. |
| MCP | One program to one agent, over standard input and output, or over HTTP. |
| Front end | Several installed programs over one HTTP port, as MCP tools and a JSON API, with optional eval. Each program runs in its own daemon, which the front end starts on first use. |

`mim` always serves through the front end. It names the programs to serve explicitly; nothing is served because it happens to be installed. The front end finds each program’s manifest in the installed-programs directory of the state ([Overview](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/ecosystem-architecture/eco-overview.md)), checks every one at startup, and starts each program’s daemon on its first request. A daemon that has exited is started again on the next request for it, and so is a live one whose socket has gone; a daemon that only refuses a connection is left running, since a full connection backlog refuses too. Requests to one program run concurrently: the front end serializes only the reaping and starting of a program’s daemon, never the exchange of a request with it. An MCP server over HTTP likewise runs its calls concurrently, up to the daemon’s own number of workers, and its other methods never wait behind a call.

## 11.8.2. Endpoints

The front end answers:

| Request | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `GET /health` | Liveness. Open to every caller, so a monitor needs no secret. |
| `POST /mcp` | The MCP endpoint. |
| `POST /call/<module>/<command>` | Call one command. The body is the arguments as a JSON array in order, or an object whose `args` is that array or an object keyed by argument name. `?render=<action>` selects an output action. |
| `GET /discover`, `GET /discover/<module>` | The served modules, then one module’s commands with their arguments, types and documentation. |
| `POST /eval` | Evaluate an expression, when eval is enabled (below). |

A call by name may leave out any argument the command line lets you leave out, and the server fills it as the command line would: an option takes its default, a flag its declared default, a record its fields' defaults, an optional positional `null`. Names are the arguments' published names (below). An unknown name, a name given twice and a flag that is not a boolean are refused. An argument the command line may read from standard input is required, since a remote caller has none to give; a path names a file on the server. With no `render`, the command’s default output action runs, as on the command line; `raw` selects the function’s own value.

A successful call returns `{"status":"ok","result":...}`. A command whose result carries a media type returns the raw bytes with that type instead. A failure returns `{"status":"error","class":"...","error":"..."}`, and the class sets the HTTP status: `bad-request` 400, `not-found` 404, `limit` 413, `failure` 500, `reply-limit` 500, `recovering` 503 with `Retry-After`, and `unauthorized` 401 or `forbidden` 403 for the token rules below. A forwarded failure keeps the class its daemon gave it.

A request larger than the server takes is answered with `limit`, never dropped: a daemon takes 64 MiB on its socket and 4 MiB over HTTP, the front end and the MCP server 64 MiB, and the front end refuses, without forwarding it, a request its daemon would not take. A reply too large for the socket protocol’s 4 GiB frame is a `reply-limit` failure.

## 11.8.3. Commands as MCP tools

Each exported command of each program on the MCP view becomes one tool, named `<module>__<command>`. A name that collides is refused at startup. The tool’s description is the command’s documentation, and its input schema is an object with one property per argument, keyed by the argument’s published name (its declared long name, or `_1`, `_2`, …​ for positional arguments). Morloc types map to JSON Schema:

| Morloc type | JSON Schema |
| --- | --- |
| `Bool` | `boolean` |
| integer types | `integer` |
| real types | `number` |
| `Str` | `string` |
| enumerations | `string` with `enum` |
| sum types | `oneOf` a constructor-name string or a one-key object |
| lists, tables | `array` |
| tuples | `array` with fixed `prefixItems` |
| records | `object`, required fields being those not optional |
| optional `?T` | `T` or `null`, never required |

A record argument is offered by its fields, one property each, and also whole, under its own name, where the command line takes it whole; a field given by name overrides the same field of the whole record. The arguments are read by the same rules as a call by name on the JSON API, defaults included. A command with output actions gets an extra `_render` property whose values are `raw` and each action’s name, defaulting to the command’s default action, and its description lists the actions. When a command without actions returns a record, the tool also declares an output schema and returns structured content; otherwise a JSON result is one text block, an image is an image block and other media is a resource.

A command is not offered as a tool if its result is a file handle or a stream handle, which means nothing to a remote caller. A command that streams its output is offered, but a call to it is refused as invalid params: its output would go to the standard output that the transport owns, not to the caller.

**Protocol.** The server speaks MCP protocol version `2025-06-18`. A client sends `initialize`, then the `notifications/initialized` notification; `tools/list` and `tools/call` before that are rejected. Over HTTP, `initialize` returns an `Mcp-Session-Id` header that every later request must carry; an unknown session is told to initialize again, and an idle session expires. A call that fails while running returns a normal result marked `isError`, with the message as text. A message that is not JSON is a JSON-RPC parse error; an unknown tool or a bad argument is an invalid-params error; a request past a size limit is an invalid-request error (over HTTP, a body past the cap is answered 413 before it is read as JSON-RPC).

## 11.8.4. Pool crash recovery

A daemon outlives any one call, so it must survive a pool that crashes. When it finds a pool dead, it closes admission (new requests are answered as unavailable, HTTP 503), stops every pool, and waits for the requests already running to finish. It then stops the writer of every open output stream, which ends each file with a `failed` status ([Streaming and memory mapping](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-streaming.md)). Only then does it discard the program’s shared memory, create it afresh, restart and ping every pool, and reopen admission. No request spans a recovery, so no shared-memory reference from before the crash is ever read after it. If running requests do not finish within a minute, or recovery keeps failing, the daemon exits instead of serving from an inconsistent state.

## 11.8.5. Eval

When enabled, eval lets a caller send a whole Morloc expression that composes installed functions. It is offered as `POST /eval` with `{"expr": "..."}` and as an MCP tool named `eval` whose description lists the importable modules.

Each request is typechecked, compiled and run in a fresh process group, under these restrictions:

-   Every `import` must name a module on the **allow-list**, checked against the module’s real name, so renaming on import does not help.
-   Only installed modules resolve; local imports are refused.
-   The expression may not source foreign code or declare types, typeclasses or instances.
-   Input and output intrinsics may not appear directly; a function from an allowed module may still perform them, so the reachable I/O is exactly what those modules export.
-   The compiler’s memory is capped at 2 GB; CPU time at a configurable limit (30 seconds by default) and wall time at four times that. A request over its limit has its whole process group stopped.

Nothing about one request is kept for the next.

## 11.8.6. Security model

A server binds the loopback address unless told otherwise, so only the local machine can reach it. A server bound to any other address must have a **token**, a shared secret every request presents as `Authorization: Bearer <token>`; without it a request is refused with 401. The token is compared in constant time, and only `/health` is exempt. Starting an exposed server without a token requires an explicit waiver, meant for a gateway that already checks callers.

Eval is code execution, so it is held to a stricter rule: with no token it is **locked** — not listed, reported as locked by `/discover`, and refused — unless waived separately from the server-wide waiver. `mim` grants that waiver to a loopback server, where every caller is already local.

Remote clients are untrusted in other ways too: a request must arrive within a deadline, its headers and body are bounded, and the number of simultaneous connections is capped, so one client cannot exhaust the server.

The plain-HTTP server does not encrypt. A token stops strangers who find the port, not anyone who can watch the network; `mim` therefore requires the operator to acknowledge plaintext before exposing a server, and an untrusted network needs a tunnel or a TLS proxy in front.

## 11.8.7. Serving an environment

`mim` keeps, per environment, a **view** for each adapter — the modules answering over MCP and over the JSON API — and an optional eval allow-list. Installing a module never serves it. `mim start` reads the views, starts one front end for the environment, and records its process or container. A second `start` is refused while the recorded server is alive (judged by the recorded process being the one `mim` started, not merely a live process id), unless told to replace it. `stop` ends the server and removes the record.

The token is chosen by the operator and passed to the server in its environment. `mim` never generates one, writes one to disk, or puts one on a command line. A container server runs with a read-only root file system, and the environment is marked immutable while it serves ([Environment solving](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/ecosystem-architecture/eco-solving.md)), so a caller cannot change the installed software.


---

<!-- https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/ecosystem-architecture/eco-freezing.html -->

# 11.9. Freezing

Morloc Manual > Ecosystem Architecture | https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/ecosystem-architecture/eco-freezing.html | prev: https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/ecosystem-architecture/eco-serving.md | next: https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/index.md

> An environment changes as programs are installed and packages solved. **Freezing** captures it as it stands in a container image that runs the same programs and serves the same views on another machine, with nothing mounted from the machine that built it. This section specifies what a frozen image contains, what it requires of its host, how it decides who may reach it, and what a slim image gives up.

**Which environments.** Only a Docker or Podman environment provisioned from a release can be frozen. A native or Apptainer environment has no image to build on, and a development environment’s compiler lives outside it. The image is built by the environment’s own engine, on the machine that holds the environment, and freezing changes nothing in the environment.

**Contents.** The image is the environment’s image with:

-   the toolchain installed from the environment’s lock, without solving again, so its packages are exactly those the environment was tested with; a lock that does not install fails the freeze;
-   the Morloc home ([Overview](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/ecosystem-architecture/eco-overview.md));
-   every installed program, with its build directory and its copied source directory, and the installed module source;
-   the views and eval allow-list, as the image’s default command.

An environment that is missing any of these, for instance because it was never fully built, is refused with the missing part named.

**What is refused.** Each program travels as the directory `mim install` copied, so freezing inspects them first. Tool state that nothing reads at run time — version-control directories, caches, virtual environments, build output — is refused. A program over 100 MB, a file over 50 MB, or an environment with no programs at all must be confirmed by the user; without a terminal to ask, confirmation is refusal. A force option answers all of these.

**Running the image.** The default command starts the front end ([Serving](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/ecosystem-architecture/eco-serving.md)) listening on every interface on port 8080. Inside a container that is the only way a published port can reach it, so the image does not decide who can reach it: whoever runs it does, with the port mapping and the network. A token, if given at run time in `MORLOC_MCP_TOKEN`, is required exactly as on any server. Eval stays locked without a token unless `MORLOC_EVAL_ALLOW_NO_AUTH` is set. An environment with no views gives an image with no default command; its programs run when named.

Morloc moves data between pools through shared memory, which container engines limit by default; the image records the size the environment used in a label so that the operator can grant it.

**Labels.** Once it leaves the manager nothing tracks the image, so it describes itself: the Morloc version, the source environment, the programs, each adapter’s modules, whether eval is on, and the suggested shared-memory size.

**Slim images.** A slim image omits what only building needs: compilers, the solver, the Morloc compiler, the runtime’s headers and source, and the build-only packages, found by walking the solved packages' dependencies from the requested ones without passing through a build tool. It keeps every interpreter and library the programs load, and every tool a program declares together with everything that tool depends on, even a package that would otherwise count as build-only. Since eval compiles code, an environment with eval enabled cannot be frozen slim. After a slim image is built, every program is started inside it and every runtime library’s links are resolved, so a missing library is found at freeze time rather than in production.


---

<!-- https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/ -->

# 12. Build Architecture

Morloc Manual | https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/ | prev: https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/ecosystem-architecture/eco-freezing.md | next: https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-overview.md

This chapter specifies what `morloc make` produces and how the result runs. A compiled program is a manifest describing its commands, one pool per language holding the generated code, and a launcher. At run time the nexus reads the manifest, starts the pools, and sends the first call; the pools then call one another directly. The chapter defines the process lifecycle and worker model, the protocol the processes speak, the shared memory and binary formats that data travels in, streams, how errors propagate, and the data flow through the CLI’s collection, parsing and rendering stages.


---

<!-- https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-overview.html -->

# 12.1. Runtime overview

Morloc Manual > Build Architecture | https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-overview.html | prev: https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/index.md | next: https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-artifacts.md

> A running Morloc program is a small set of cooperating processes: one **nexus** and one **pool** per language the program uses. The nexus is the program’s entry point and its only owner of shared resources. The pools execute the generated code. This section maps how they fit together; the sections that follow specify each piece.

**The nexus** is a single precompiled binary shared by every Morloc program. It reads the program’s manifest, interprets the request, starts the pools the request needs, sends the first call, and delivers the result. It runs in one of four modes:

| Mode | Behavior |
| --- | --- |
| CLI | One request from the command line, then exit. Starts only the pools the command can reach. |
| Daemon | Long-running server for many requests over a Unix socket, TCP or HTTP. Starts every pool at startup. |
| MCP | Long-running Model Context Protocol server for agents, on stdio or HTTP. Starts every pool at startup. |
| Call packet | Reads one prebuilt call from a file and writes the reply to a file. Used for jobs on cluster nodes. |

A command whose body calls no foreign function is **pure**. The nexus evaluates it itself and starts no pools.

**A pool** is one long-lived process per language. It holds every function the program uses from that language, compiled or loaded together, and serves calls on its own socket. Calls between functions in the same pool are ordinary native calls: no serialization and no IPC.

**A call that crosses languages** goes directly from the calling pool to the callee’s pool. The nexus is not on the path. A connection carries one call packet and then its reply packet at a time. A thread that calls a C++ or Rust pool keeps its connection for its next call, since setting one up costs about as much as the round trip itself; a call into Python or R opens a connection of its own.

![Diagram](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/static/img/mermaid-4494ea1c347c7e54e6bb7ab36d329fac.svg)

**Data travels in one of three ways.** Every value that leaves a process is first serialized to the language-neutral binary form described in [Voidstar format and schema strings](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-voidstar.md). Where that serialized form then goes depends on its size and on whether shared memory is available:

| Route | When |
| --- | --- |
| Inline | The serialized value is at most the inline threshold (64 KiB by default). It is copied into the packet. |
| Shared memory | The value is larger. It is written into shared memory and the packet carries a pointer to it ([Shared memory layout](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-shm.md)). |
| File | The value is larger and shared memory is disabled. It is written to a temporary file and the packet carries the path. |

A shared-memory pointer is relative: it names a block by volume and offset, so it means the same block in every process of the program. This lets a pool read a large argument where its sender wrote it, without a copy across the socket.

**Ownership.** The nexus creates the program’s shared-memory namespace and temporary directory, and it alone removes them. It is also the only writer of every output stream and of standard output: pools hand it their batches through shared memory, and it writes the files ([Streaming and memory mapping](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-streaming.md)). Each pool watches a pipe whose write end only the nexus holds, and exits when the nexus does. Startup, shutdown and crash handling are specified in [Process lifecycle](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-lifecycle.md).


---

<!-- https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-artifacts.html -->

# 12.2. Compilation artifacts
