Morloc Manual > Build Architecture | https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-artifacts.html | prev: https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-overview.md | next: https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-lifecycle.md

> `morloc make` turns a Morloc program into a build directory and one or more launchers. The build directory holds the generated pools and a manifest that describes every command. A launcher is a short shell script that hands the manifest to the nexus. This section specifies that layout, the manifest, and what installing a program does.

**Layout.** A program is identified by a **key**: the `--name` given, else the `-o` name, else the source file’s base name. Building `demo.loc` that calls Python and C++ produces:

```
./
|-- demo                  CLI launcher
|-- demo.loc, foo.py ...  the program's sources (not copied)
`-- demo-build/
    |-- .morloc-build     marker: this directory is a Morloc build
    |-- manifest.json     commands, pools and runtime settings
    |-- envspec.json      dependencies, for the environment manager
    `-- pools/
        |-- cpp/          generated source and the compiled pool binary
        `-- py/           generated pool script
```

Compiled languages (C++, Rust) are built into a pool binary. Interpreted languages (Python, R) get a generated script that loads the user’s source files when it starts. Those files are found relative to the build directory, in the directory that contains it. The build directory and its source directory therefore move together; neither is relocatable alone. No absolute build path is recorded.

**Rebuilds** assemble the new tree in a sibling staging directory and move it into place only after every pool compiles. A failed build leaves the previous build in place. A rebuild deletes an existing `<key>-build` directory only if it carries the marker file, so a user directory that happens to have the same name is never removed.

**Launchers.** Each launcher records the manifest path on a comment line (`# morloc-manifest: demo-build/manifest.json`), resolves its own location, and execs the nexus with a mode and the manifest:

| Launcher | Created by | Runs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| CLI | default (`-o` names it, `--no-cli` suppresses it) | `morloc-nexus run <manifest> ...` |
| Daemon | `--daemon-out NAME` | `morloc-nexus daemon <manifest> ...` |

There is no MCP launcher. `morloc-nexus mcp` takes either launcher or the manifest itself as its target. Every nexus mode that names a program accepts both forms.

**The manifest** is a JSON object written by the compiler and read only by the nexus. Its main fields:

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `name` | Program name. |
| `build` | Compiler version, build time, and the build directory (always `.`, the manifest’s own directory). |
| `pools` | One entry per language: the command line that starts the pool, relative to the build directory, and the pool’s socket name. |
| `commands` | One entry per exported function (below). |
| `groups` | Named groups of commands for the CLI. |
| `inline_size`, `no_shm`, `tmpdir` | Data-route settings fixed at build time ([Runtime overview](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-overview.md)). |
| `run_log` | Prologue and epilogue templates for the run log ([Logs and result caching](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-runs.md)). |

Each command records its name, its documentation, its arguments and return value, and either how to run it or the expression itself:

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `type` | `remote` (runs in a pool) or `pure` (the nexus evaluates `expr` itself). |
| `mid`, `pool` | For `remote`: the function’s index inside its pool, and which pool holds it. |
| `needed_pools` | Every pool the command can reach, so a CLI run starts only those. |
| `args`, `return` | Each with its Morloc type and its schema string, which fixes the binary layout of the value ([Voidstar format and schema strings](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-voidstar.md)). |

The manifest carries no schema version of its own. The nexus accepts a manifest only if it was written by the same Morloc version, and refuses any other with a message to rebuild. Builds are artifacts, regenerated on every `make`, so an exact match costs nothing and removes every cross-version compatibility question. Within a version, readers ignore keys they do not know. Every entity also carries an empty `constraints` list and `metadata` object, reserved so that later additions need no format change.

**Installing** (`morloc make --install`, or `morloc install --build`) builds into the Morloc home rather than the working directory. The program’s key is its module name. The source directory is mirrored to `exe/<module>/`, skipping version-control data, paths listed in a `.morlocignore` file, and stale build directories (found by their marker). The build lands in `exe/<module>/<module>-build/`, and the CLI launcher is copied to `bin/`, which you put on your `PATH`. A reinstall requires `--force`, and replaces the whole mirrored tree.


---

<!-- https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-lifecycle.html -->

# 12.3. Process lifecycle

Morloc Manual > Build Architecture | https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-lifecycle.html | prev: https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-artifacts.md | next: https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-workers.md

> A run creates processes, a private directory and shared memory, and must remove all of them however it ends: normally, by error, by signal, or by being killed outright. This section specifies how a run starts its pools, how it knows they are ready, how it stops them, and what it guarantees about cleanup and exit status.

**Startup.** Before it starts any pool, the nexus:

1.  Creates the **run directory**, a fresh directory under `/tmp` readable only by the user, and writes an owner record into it (the nexus’s pid, process start time, boot id and pid namespace). It always lives under `/tmp` so a later run can find it; the owner record tells a dead run from a live one.
2.  Removes the run directories and shared memory of earlier runs whose owner is dead and whose pools have all ended.
3.  Creates the run’s shared memory: the first volume and the stream registry ([Shared memory layout](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-shm.md)).
4.  Installs its signal handlers.

It then starts each pool the request needs ([Runtime overview](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-overview.md)):

1.  It starts a **pin**: a tiny process that leads a new process group, ignores termination signals, and exits only when the nexus closes a pipe to it. The pin holds the group’s id, so the id cannot be reissued to an unrelated process while the nexus may still signal the group.
2.  It records the group in the run directory, then starts the pool inside that group. The pool’s command line is the manifest’s command for it followed by three arguments: its socket path, the run directory, and the shared-memory base name. The pool inherits the nexus’s standard input, output and error unchanged.
3.  It pings each pool on its socket until one answers with a ping packet ([Packet protocol](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-packets.md)). Retries back off exponentially. If the pool process exits first, startup fails at once and reports its exit status.

**The lifeline.** The nexus holds the only write end of a pipe; every pool receives the read end. The kernel closes the write end when the nexus exits for any reason, including `SIGKILL`, so a pool always learns that its nexus is gone. It then ends its own process group (`SIGTERM`, 200 ms, `SIGKILL`) and starts a detached **sweeper** that removes the run’s shared memory and directory once every recorded group has ended. Without the lifeline, a killed nexus would leave pools and shared memory behind indefinitely.

**Shutdown.** At the end of a successful run the nexus first finishes standard output and error and discards any output stream the program left open ([Streaming and memory mapping](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-streaming.md)). At the end of any run, or on `SIGINT`, `SIGTERM` or `SIGHUP`, it then stops its pools: `SIGTERM` to every pool group, up to 200 ms for the pool processes to exit, then `SIGKILL` to every group. It then removes the names of the shared-memory objects and the run directory. It removes names but never unmaps memory at exit, because a background thread may still be reading it. When a pool process exits on its own, the nexus kills the rest of its group, so a pool’s worker processes never outlive it.

**Cleanup on every path:**

| How the run ends | Who removes shared memory and the run directory |
| --- | --- |
| Normal exit, error, `SIGINT`/`SIGTERM`/`SIGHUP` | The nexus, before it exits. |
| Crash signal (`SIGSEGV`, `SIGBUS`, `SIGFPE`, `SIGABRT`) | The nexus’s crash handler removes the shared memory, then the signal takes its default action. |
| Internal error (panic) | The nexus kills its pool groups and removes what it registered before exiting. |
| `SIGKILL` or power loss of the nexus | Each pool’s sweeper, after its lifeline closes; failing that, the next run’s startup sweep. |

A long-running daemon additionally recovers from a pool crash by stopping every pool, waiting for running requests, discarding the shared memory and starting fresh; that is specified with the daemon in [Serving](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/ecosystem-architecture/eco-serving.md).

**Exit status** of a one-shot run:

| Status | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| 0 | Success. |
| 1 | The call failed: an error raised by user code, a pool that died, an argument that could not be read, or a runtime error. |
| 2 | Usage error: an unknown command or option. |
| 70 | Internal error: an invariant inside Morloc itself was broken (a panic). Only a panic exits with 70. |
| 128 + *N* | Ended by signal *N* (130 for `SIGINT`, 143 for `SIGTERM`). |
| 141 | Standard output was a closed pipe (128 + `SIGPIPE`), as when the output is piped to `head`. |


---

<!-- https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-workers.html -->

# 12.4. Worker model

Morloc Manual > Build Architecture | https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-workers.html | prev: https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-lifecycle.md | next: https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-packets.md

> A pool serves many calls at once: concurrent requests to a daemon, parallel maps, and calls that come back into a pool while it is already waiting on another. This section specifies how the nexus and the pools divide that work among threads and processes, how pools grow and shrink, and the one rule that keeps calls between pools from deadlocking.

**The nexus.** A one-shot nexus makes one call and waits for it. A daemon runs an accept thread and a fixed set of request workers (four more than the number of pools, between 4 and 32); a request waits in a queue until a worker is free. An MCP server over HTTP serves up to 128 connections, each on its own thread, and runs at most as many `tools/call` requests at once as a daemon has workers. In every mode, a `SIGCHLD` handler reaps child processes as they exit, so a pool’s death is noticed at once, and each open output stream has a writer thread with its compression jobs ([Streaming and memory mapping](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-streaming.md)).

**Pools.** Each pool has one process that owns its socket, and a set of **workers** that run user code. How a worker is made depends on the language:

| Language | Workers |
| --- | --- |
| C++, Rust | Threads. An accept thread queues each connection; a worker thread takes it. |
| Python | Forked processes. A coordinator process, which loads no user code and runs no threads, binds the pool’s socket and forks the workers; each worker loads the user’s sources after the fork, and idle workers accept on the socket directly. |
| R | Forked processes. Idle workers accept on the pool’s socket directly. |

Forked workers are created only from a process with a single thread, because a forked child inherits only the thread that forked it, and any lock another thread held at that moment would stay locked forever. Loading user code after the fork keeps libraries that start their own threads out of the coordinator.

**The no-deadlock rule.** A pool never leaves an incoming call waiting while every one of its workers is blocked on another pool. Cross-language calls can nest in any pattern: a Python function calls C++, which calls back into Python. If the only Python worker were waiting on C++, the callback would wait forever. So:

-   A thread pool starts a new worker whenever a call arrives and no worker is free.
-   A forked pool counts a worker as blocked while it waits on another pool (a foreign call, or a read or write on a channel), and forks a new worker when every worker is blocked. A call that arrives while some worker is merely computing waits for it.

Calls that arrive one after another reuse a single worker; only real concurrency adds workers. There is no upper bound, because any bound would reintroduce the deadlock.

**Shrinking.** Each pool starts with one worker. A worker beyond the first that stays idle for 60 seconds exits (`MORLOC_POOL_IDLE_TIMEOUT_MS` changes this), so a burst of concurrency is not paid for again if it recurs within a minute, and a one-off spike is not kept for the rest of the run. A worker decides to leave itself, and only while it holds no shared memory, since memory a killed worker still held could not be recovered. R workers never exit before the pool does.

**Ordering.** A connection carries one request and then its reply at a time, and belongs to one calling thread, so a reply always reaches the caller that asked. A kept connection (C++ and Rust pools) holds its worker, which waits for that connection’s next call and takes no other; calls on new connections still get a free worker or a new one, so the no-deadlock rule holds. Concurrent calls have no ordering guarantee relative to one another. A pool’s own sequential code (a `map` in one worker, say) runs in order.

**Locks.** State shared between processes is guarded by locks that survive the death of their holder: if a process dies holding one, the next process to take it is told, and treats what it protects as damaged rather than waiting forever ([Shared memory layout](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-shm.md)). Within a process, locks are always taken in one global order, so two threads can never each hold a lock the other wants.


---

<!-- https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-packets.html -->

# 12.5. Packet protocol

Morloc Manual > Build Architecture | https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-packets.html | prev: https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-workers.md | next: https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-shm.md

> Every message between Morloc processes is a **packet**: a fixed 32-byte header, optional metadata, and a payload. The same format carries calls, results, errors and readiness pings over sockets, and it is also the on-disk format of streams and cached results. This section specifies the header, each packet type, metadata blocks, how a payload names its data, and the transport rules.

**Layout.** A packet is a header, then `offset` bytes of metadata, then `length` bytes of payload. All integers are little-endian.

| Offset | Size | Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | 4 | magic | `0x0707f86d` (bytes `6d f8 07 07`). A packet without it is rejected. |
| 4 | 2 | plain | Reserved, 0. |
| 6 | 2 | version | Reserved, 0. |
| 8 | 2 | flavor | Reserved, 0. |
| 10 | 2 | mode | Bit 0 on a call: the caller can reuse the connection; on the reply: the callee keeps it. Other bits 0. |
| 12 | 8 | command | Packet type (first byte) and type-specific fields. |
| 20 | 4 | offset | Bytes of metadata between the header and the payload. |
| 24 | 8 | length | Bytes of payload. |

**Packet types**, from the first command byte:

| Type | Name | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | data | A value, or an error. |
| 1 | call | A function call: which function, and its arguments. |
| 2 | ping | Readiness check. The header alone; the reply is an identical ping. |
| 3 | stream | Opens a stream file; the length field is all ones, since a stream has no fixed length ([Streaming and memory mapping](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-streaming.md)). |
| 4 | footer | Closes a stream file with its index ([Streaming and memory mapping](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-streaming.md)). |

A **call** carries the function’s index inside the receiving pool (the `mid` from the manifest) as a 32-bit integer at byte 16, and an entry-point byte at byte 13: 0 for an ordinary call, 1 for a call read from a file, as on a cluster node. Its payload is the arguments, each a complete data packet, concatenated in order. The receiver walks them by their own sizes.

A **data** packet describes its payload in the command field:

| Byte | Field | Values |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 13 | source | 0 inline: the payload is the value. 1 file: the payload is a path. 2 pointer: the payload is an 8-byte relative pointer into shared memory ([Shared memory layout](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-shm.md)). |
| 14 | format | 0 JSON, 1 MessagePack, 2 text, 3 packet (the file is itself a packet or stream), 4 voidstar ([Voidstar format and schema strings](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-voidstar.md)), 5 Arrow ([Tables and tensors on the wire](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-tables.md)). |
| 15 | compression | 0 none, 1 Zstandard. |
| 16 | encryption | Reserved, 0. |
| 17 | status | 0 pass, 1 fail, 2 output pipe closed. |
| 18-19 | generation | For a pointer, the generation of the shared-memory block it names ([Shared memory layout](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-shm.md)), little-endian; never 0, and a pointer packet recording 0 is refused. |

Not every combination is meaningful. Values crossing between pools use inline or pointer voidstar; tables use pointer Arrow; values in temporary files (shared memory disabled) use file MessagePack.

**Errors** are data packets with status 1, inline source and text format; the payload is the error message, including its cross-language traceback ([Error propagation](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-errors.md)). Status 2 marks a write to a closed standard output, so the nexus can end the run with the conventional broken-pipe status instead of an error. A pool answers every call with exactly one packet: a request it cannot even read is answered with an error packet rather than silence.

**Metadata** is a sequence of blocks. Each block is the three bytes `mmh`, a one-byte kind, a 32-bit body size, then the body. Readers stop at the first block that does not start with `mmh`, and the region is zero-padded to a multiple of 32 bytes.

| Kind | Name | Body |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | schema | The schema string of the payload’s type, NUL-terminated ([Voidstar format and schema strings](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-voidstar.md)). |
| 3 | volume index | A 16-bit shared-memory volume index. |
| 4 | frame index | Sizes of the payload’s compressed frames; required when compression is Zstandard. |
| 5 | subpacket index | Offsets and element counts of a stream’s batches. |
| 6, 7, 8 | stream diagnostics, final footer, footer status | Used only in stream files ([Streaming and memory mapping](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-streaming.md)). |

A packet between pools needs no schema block, because both sides know the type from the compiled program. Packets written to disk carry one, so that any tool can read them without the program that wrote them.

**Transport.** Packets travel over Unix-domain stream sockets. A connection carries one call packet and then its reply at a time; a caller thread keeps one connection to each C++ or Rust pool for its later calls, while Python and R pools close the connection after each reply. There is no separate framing: the receiver reads the 32-byte header and then exactly `offset + length` more bytes. Before a pointer payload is sent, the sender takes a shared-memory reference on the receiver’s behalf, so the block cannot be freed in the gap before the receiver reads it; if the send fails, the sender drops that reference again.

A caller waits for a reply as long as the callee lives, with no deadline: a call may legitimately run for days. A pool reading a request waits as long as the sending process exists, checking once a second.


---

<!-- https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-shm.html -->

# 12.6. Shared memory layout

Morloc Manual > Build Architecture | https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-shm.html | prev: https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-packets.md | next: https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-voidstar.md

> Large values pass between pools through shared memory, so a value written by one process can be read by another where it lies, with only an 8-byte pointer crossing the socket. This section specifies the shared-memory volumes and blocks of a run, the pointer forms that address them, and the rules for allocating, sharing and releasing a block among processes that may die at any moment.

**Volumes.** A run’s shared memory is a set of **volumes**, each a POSIX shared-memory object mapped by every process of the run. Volume *i* is named `<base>-<i>` with *i* as four hex digits, where the nexus chooses the base name (`/mlc-<pid>-<random>-<generation>`) and passes it to every pool. The generation changes when a daemon discards its shared memory and starts over, so the new namespace never collides with the old. Volume 0 is never created: index 0 is reserved for pointers into a self-contained buffer ([Voidstar format and schema strings](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-voidstar.md)). The first volume is index 1, with 64 KiB of data; a process that needs more creates another volume at an unused index, at least twice the size of the largest volume it has mapped, up to 32767 volumes. If the shared-memory filesystem is full or unavailable, a volume is created as a file in the run directory instead, and a zero-length stub under the shared-memory name tells other processes where it is.

Each volume starts with a header:

| Offset | Size | Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | 4 | magic | `0xFECA0DF0`, written last by the creator; a volume without it is not ready. |
| 4 | 128 | name | The volume’s name, NUL-padded. |
| 132 | 4 | index | The volume’s index, checked when a process opens it. |
| 136 | 8 | size | Bytes of data after the header. |
| 144 | 8 | poison | Nonzero when the program fills released blocks with a poison byte (`MORLOC_SHM_POISON=1`); the primary volume’s value holds for every process. |
| 152 | \- | lock | A process-shared lock guarding the block list (size set by the platform). |
| \- | 8 | cursor | Offset of the block where the next search starts, or -1. |
| \- | 4 | next index | In the primary volume, the program’s volumes are numbered below this. |
| \- | \- | growth lock | A process-shared lock taken to create the next volume. |

The header is padded to a multiple of 16 bytes, and the data region follows it. Volumes never leave the machine, so the platform’s own lock layout is acceptable.

**Blocks.** The data region is a sequence of blocks, each a 16-byte header followed by its data:

| Offset | Size | Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | 4 | magic | `0x0CB10DF0` for a block; a header merged into a neighbor is zeroed. |
| 4 | 4 | references | 0 when free; all ones while the last reference is being dropped. |
| 8 | 8 | size | Bytes of data in the low 48 bits; its generation, advanced each time the block is allocated, in the top 16. |

Block data is 16-byte aligned and its size a multiple of 16, because some Arrow column types hold 128-bit words that another language’s Arrow library will read in place and expects aligned. To allocate, a process takes the volume’s lock, searches next-fit from the cursor (merging adjacent free blocks as it passes them), splits off any usable remainder as a new free block, and sets the block’s count from 0 to 1. It tries the volume it used last, then the others, then creates a new volume.

**Pointers.** Three forms address shared memory:

| Form | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Relative | Volume index in bits 62-48 and offset into that volume’s data in bits 47-0; -1 is null ([Voidstar format and schema strings](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-voidstar.md)). The same in every process; this is the only form that crosses a process boundary. |
| Volume | An offset into one volume’s data region. Used inside a volume, for its cursor. |
| Absolute | An address in this process. Never stored in shared memory, since each process maps the volumes at different addresses. |

Converting a relative pointer to an absolute one maps the named volume on first use, so a process can follow a pointer into a volume another process created after it started.

**References.** A block’s count is the number of holders that may still read it. The allocator holds the first reference. A process sending a pointer to another takes a reference for the receiver before sending ([Packet protocol](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-packets.md)), and the receiver owns it on arrival. Taking a reference on a block that is free or being released fails rather than reviving it. The last release overwrites the block’s data with zeros before marking it free, so a stale reader sees zeros instead of another value. A count names no holder, so the references of a process that died cannot be found and released one by one; they are recovered only by discarding the whole namespace, which the end of a run, or a daemon’s recovery, does.

**Concurrency.** Each volume’s lock is **robust**: if a process dies holding it, the next process to take it is told so. The volume’s block list may then be half edited, so the volume is marked damaged and never allocated from again; allocation moves on to another volume. A volume is created with exclusive creation, so when two processes race to create the same index one wins and the other opens the winner’s volume once its magic appears.

**Removal.** The process that created the first volume (the nexus) removes the names of all volumes when the run ends ([Process lifecycle](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-lifecycle.md)). It never unmaps them while threads may still read; the kernel frees the memory once the last process unmaps it.


---

<!-- https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-voidstar.html -->

# 12.7. Voidstar format and schema strings

Morloc Manual > Build Architecture | https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-voidstar.html | prev: https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-shm.md | next: https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-tables.md

> **Voidstar** is the binary layout every value takes when it leaves a language: C-like fixed-width slots, with variable-length parts reached through relative pointers. A **schema string** is a compact description of a type’s layout. A buffer plus its schema is enough for any language to read the value, with no other type information. Every binding reads and writes this one layout, so a value crosses between any two languages with no intermediate format.

## 12.7.1. Schema strings

A schema is a string of type codes in prefix order. Codes that take children are followed by them; codes that take a count are followed by it.

| Code | Type | Followed by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `z` | Unit | nothing |
| `b` | Bool | nothing |
| `i1` `i2` `i4` `i8` | Signed integer of 1, 2, 4, 8 bytes | \- |
| `u1` `u2` `u4` `u8` | Unsigned integer | \- |
| `f4` `f8` | Float (`Real` is `f8`) | \- |
| `j` | `Int`, arbitrary precision | nothing |
| `s` | String (UTF-8) | nothing |
| `a` | Array | the element schema; `a:N` declares the length as decimal *N* |
| `t` | Tuple | count, then each element schema |
| `m` | Record | count, then for each field its name and schema |
| `?` | Optional | the inner schema |
| `e` | Enum (no constructor has fields) | count, then constructor names |
| `v` | Variant (sum type) | count, then for each arm its name, field count and field schemas |
| `T` | Table ([Tables and tensors on the wire](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-tables.md)) | optionally `:` count, then column names and schemas |
| `F` `O` `I` | Input file, output stream, input stream ([Streaming and memory mapping](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-streaming.md)) | nothing |
| `&` | Names the schema that follows, for recursion | name, then the schema |
| `^` | Refers back to an enclosing `&` | name |

Counts and name lengths are base-64 numbers. A value below 64 is one digit from `0-9`, `a-z`, `A-Z`, `+`, `/` (0 to 63). A larger value is written as `=`, its low digit, and the rest of the number, recursively: 100 is `=A1`. Names are written as their length followed by their bytes. Enums and variants have at most 256 constructors, and nesting is limited to 128 levels.

A schema may also carry **hints** in angle brackets (`<dict>`) naming the concrete type a language should build. Hints do not change the layout and are dropped from the canonical form stored in packets.

Examples, from real programs:

| Schema | Type |
| --- | --- |
| `j` | `Int` |
| `v23Err1s2Ok1z` | `Try Str ()`: arm `Err` with one `s` field, arm `Ok` with one `z` field |
| `m24names2idi4` | `{name :: Str, id :: I32}` |
| `&4Treev24Leaf04Node24Tree4Tree` | `data Tree = Leaf \| Node Tree Tree` |
| `t3sjaau1` | A function value: home language, function index, captured values as packets |

## 12.7.2. Layout

Every value has a fixed-width **slot**. Integers are little-endian.

| Code | Width | Align | Slot contents |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `z` | 0 | 1 | Nothing. |
| `b`, `i1`, `u1` | 1 | 1 | The value. |
| `i2` …​ `f8` | 2, 4, 8 | natural | The value. |
| `e` | 1 | 1 | Constructor ordinal, in declaration order. |
| `s`, `a` | 16 | 8 | 8-byte count (bytes for a string, with no NUL; elements for an array), then a relative pointer to the data. An empty one holds the null pointer. |
| `j` | 16 | 8 | 8-byte limb count, then a word. With one limb the word is the value itself. With more, it points to that many 64-bit limbs, least significant first, in two’s complement. |
| `t`, `m` | computed | `t`: largest field; `m`: 8 | C struct rules: each field at the next offset aligned for it, total rounded up to the largest field alignment. Field names exist only in the schema. |
| `?` | 8 | 8 | A relative pointer to the value, or null when absent. |
| `v` | 16 | 8 | Byte 0 is the arm’s ordinal, bytes 1-7 zero, bytes 8-15 a pointer to the arm’s fields laid out as a tuple. An arm with no fields stores null. |

Array elements are packed at the element’s width. The data of an array of numbers starts on a 64-byte boundary, so a binding can hand it to vector instructions or a numeric library without copying. A record `{name :: Str, age :: I32}` puts `name` at offset 0 and `age` at 16, with width 24.

Variant and optional slots hold a pointer rather than the value itself so that every slot’s width is fixed. This is what lets a recursive type exist: a `Tree` slot is 16 bytes however deep the tree goes. For the same reason, a type may refer to itself only through an array, optional or variant.

**Relative pointers.** A pointer is a signed 64-bit integer. Bits 62-48 name a shared-memory volume and bits 47-0 an offset into it ([Shared memory layout](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-shm.md)); -1 is null. Because a pointer names a volume rather than an address, it means the same thing in every process that maps the volumes. When a value is copied out of shared memory into one self-contained buffer (to send inline or write to disk), its pointers use volume 0 and are offsets from the start of the buffer; loading the buffer back into shared memory rebases them.

**Reading a value** takes only the schema and the buffer: the schema gives each slot’s width and each field’s offset, a pointer is followed to reach variable-length data, and a variant’s tag selects which arm’s schema governs its payload.

**Other encodings.** A value can also be written as JSON or MessagePack, for the command line, files and caches. MessagePack writes tuples and records as arrays, enums as ordinals, and variants as `[tag, payload]`; JSON writes records as objects and constructors by name. Tables have neither form and travel only as Arrow.


---

<!-- https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-tables.html -->

# 12.8. Tables and tensors on the wire

Morloc Manual > Build Architecture | https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-tables.html | prev: https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-voidstar.md | next: https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-streaming.md

> Tables are columnar, and every language with a serious table library already agrees on one columnar memory format: Apache Arrow. So a table does not travel as voidstar. It travels as Arrow data laid out in one shared-memory block, which each language imports without copying. This section specifies that block, how a table’s declared columns constrain it, and how tensors, which are ordinary voidstar values, carry their dimensions.

**The table block.** A table is always the whole value of a data packet, sent by pointer with format Arrow ([Packet protocol](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-packets.md)), even when shared memory is otherwise disabled. Tables cannot be nested inside other values. The block holds a header, then node descriptors, buffer descriptors, a string table, and the data buffers, each buffer aligned to 64 bytes from the start of the block, with zeroed padding.

| Offset | Size | Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | 4 | magic | `0xA770DA7A`. |
| 4 | 4 | version | 2\. Any other version is rejected. |
| 8 | 4 | columns | Number of columns; equals the root node’s child count. |
| 12 | 4 | nodes | Number of node descriptors. |
| 16 | 8 | rows | Number of rows; equals the root node’s length. |
| 24 | 8 | total size | Bytes in the block; every offset is checked against it. |
| 32 | 8 | metadata offset | Reserved, 0. |
| 40 | 4 | metadata length | Reserved, 0. |
| 44 | 4 | buffers | Number of buffer descriptors. |
| 48 | 4 | nodes offset | Where the node descriptors start. |
| 52 | 4 | buffers offset | Where the buffer descriptors start. |
| 56 | 4 | strings offset | Where the string table starts. |
| 60 | 4 | strings length | Bytes in the string table. |

A **node** is one Arrow array: the root is a struct whose children are the columns, and a nested column has nodes of its own. Each 64-byte node descriptor carries what the Arrow C Data Interface needs to rebuild the array: length, null count, flags, the format string and column name (as offsets into the string table), and the index and count of its buffers and children. Each 32-byte buffer descriptor gives a buffer’s offset and size within the block. Slices are compacted and dictionaries decoded before a table is written, so every node starts at offset 0 and has no dictionary.

**Zero-copy import.** A receiver validates the block (every offset in bounds, every buffer long enough for its node), then builds Arrow C Data Interface structures whose buffers point into the block, holding a reference on it for as long as the table lives. Python receives a `pyarrow` record batch, R an `arrow` record batch, C++ a nanoarrow-based handle, and Rust an `arrow-rs` record batch, each without copying the data. Converting further, to a pandas or R data frame, is the language library’s own copy. Sending a table writes a new block, except that a pool returning a table it received, unchanged, passes the same block on.

**Declared columns.** A table’s type lists columns (`T:` in its schema; [Voidstar format and schema strings](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-voidstar.md)), and that list is a lower bound: a table may have more columns, which travel after the declared ones. A declared column may be a boolean, integer, float or string, or an optional of one of these; any Arrow type may appear among the extra columns. On send, a declared column of another type is cast if the cast loses nothing, and refused otherwise. On receive, every declared column must be present with an acceptable type, and a column not declared optional must have no nulls. The number of rows is not part of the type and is not checked.

**Tables from files.** A table argument given as a file is read in the pool, not the nexus. Arrow IPC and Parquet are recognized by their magic bytes; otherwise a leading `[` or `{` marks JSON, and anything else is delimited text with a header row, split on TAB or comma by whichever names the declared columns; the file’s name is never consulted. Columns bind to declared columns by header name, and any other column is read as optional text. As output, the nexus writes a table as JSON rows, JSON lines, CSV, TSV, Arrow IPC or Parquet.

**Tensors** are not a runtime type. A tensor is a pair of its dimensions and its elements in one flat, row-major array, and travels as that ordinary voidstar tuple: `Matrix 2 2 Real` has schema `t2t2jja:4f8`. Because the array of numbers is 64-byte aligned in shared memory, Python receives a read-only numpy view over it with no copy. When the dimensions are known at compile time, the array’s length is checked against their product.


---

<!-- https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-streaming.html -->

# 12.9. Streaming and memory mapping

Morloc Manual > Build Architecture | https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-streaming.html | prev: https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-tables.md | next: https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-errors.md

> A **stream** is a list too large or too long-lived to hold in memory at once, kept in a file and read or written in batches. Any pool can read a stream another pool is writing, and a finished stream file can be read at random without loading it. This section specifies the stream file format, its compression, how processes share an open stream, how every write reaches the file through a single writer in the nexus, and what a reader may rely on while the stream is still being written.

**Stream types.** Three Morloc types name a stream, each a 16-byte slot in voidstar (schema codes `F`, `I`, `O`):

| Type | Use |
| --- | --- |
| `IFile [a]` | A finished file, read at random by element index. |
| `IStream a` | A stream read forward in batches. Several readers share one cursor, so together they consume each batch once. |
| `OStream a` | A stream written in batches. |

The slot’s first byte says what follows in its last eight: 0 for a relative pointer to a path (length, then bytes), 1 for the index of an open stream in the run’s stream registry (below). A path can cross between runs; an index means something only inside the run that opened it.

**File format.** A stream file is a sequence of packets ([Packet protocol](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-packets.md)):

| Part | Contents |
| --- | --- |
| Head | A stream packet (type 3) whose metadata holds the schema of the list, `a` followed by the element schema. Its length field is all ones. |
| Batches | Data packets, one per batch. Each payload is a self-contained voidstar array of that batch’s elements, its pointers relative to the start of the payload. |
| Footer | A footer packet (type 4) whose metadata holds a batch index (offset and element count of every batch), a final marker, and a status. |
| Tail | 8 bytes: the footer’s length as a 32-bit integer, then the magic bytes reversed (`07 07 f8 6d`). |

A reader finds the footer from the end of the file through the tail, so random access needs no scan. The status is `closed` for a stream written to the end, `paused` for one a writer stopped and may resume, or `failed` for one whose writer died in the middle of an update. While a stream is open for writing, a temporary footer carrying only diagnostics is rewritten after every batch, so the file always ends in a valid tail.

**Compression.** Each batch is compressed separately with Zstandard, so a reader can decompress any batch without the others. A batch is split into independent frames of at most 16 MiB, listed in the batch’s metadata, so they can be decompressed in parallel straight into shared memory. The user’s compression level 0-9 maps to Zstandard levels 0, 1, 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 19, 21 and 22, with long-distance matching from level 7.

**Sharing an open stream.** A stream’s identity lives in a **registry** in shared memory, created with the run’s first volume. Each slot records the file’s path, schema and element count, a write buffer, and a generation number that changes when the slot is opened and when it is released. A stream index carries the generation it was made with, and every operation checks it, so an index to a closed stream can never touch the stream that later reuses its slot. A process reading a stream keeps its own descriptor and read-only mapping of the file.

**Writing a stream.** Every output stream has exactly one writer: a thread in the nexus, started when the stream is opened. No pool opens, locks or writes the file of a stream it writes to; it only hands the nexus its elements. Standard output and standard error are written the same way.

![Diagram](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/static/img/mermaid-575da0c868de8571b65f511c685c406a.svg)

1.  `@open` and `@append` ask the nexus to open the file. It takes an exclusive lock on the file, writes the head (or, for `@append`, finds the end of the last complete batch), registers the stream and starts its writer.
2.  A `@write` from any process appends its elements to the stream’s buffer in shared memory, holding the stream’s lock only for the copy. One \`@write’s elements stay together; writes from different processes interleave only between writes, in the order they took the lock.
3.  A full buffer is moved onto the stream’s queue and replaced by an empty one, still under the lock and without touching the file. The writer takes buffers off the queue in order, compresses them on several threads (as under Compression above), and appends them to the file in queue order, so compression never reorders elements.
4.  The queue holds a bounded number of buffers (for a compressed stream, the number of compression threads clamped to 2-4, at most 7, and lowered as more streams are written; 1 for an uncompressed one). A writer that finds it full waits for the nexus, never for another pool, so streams add no way for pools to deadlock.
5.  `@flush` queues the buffered elements and returns once the nexus has written them, so a reader opened afterwards sees them. `@close` does the same and also waits for the final footer, so when it returns the file is complete, its lock is released and its path can be opened again at once.

A process that exits or dies after its `@write` returned loses nothing: its elements are already in shared memory, and the nexus writes them when the stream is flushed or closed. A process that dies while holding the stream’s lock may leave the buffer half updated; the stream is then failed, the batches queued before it are still written, and the footer says `failed`. A stream the program never closes is discarded when its index is dropped or the run ends: what was queued is written, the unflushed elements are dropped, and the file keeps its temporary footer, the sign that its writer did not finish. A daemon recovering from a pool crash ([Serving](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/ecosystem-architecture/eco-serving.md)) stops every writer before it discards shared memory, and each file ends with a `failed` status.

**Readers.** An `IFile` maps the file and locates an element through the batch index. A batch stored uncompressed and 8-byte aligned is read where it lies in the mapping; any other batch is decompressed or copied into shared memory first. An `IStream` reads forward from the shared cursor. A reader that opens a stream still being written sees the batches written before it opened, up to the temporary footer; reading past the end yields an empty batch.

**Rewriting a file.** Opening an `OStream` on a file that already has data writes a new file and renames it into place, so a reader that still has the old file mapped keeps a consistent view. Where a rename is impossible (the directory is not writable, say) and nothing in the program is reading the file, it is truncated in place instead. The runtime never deletes a stream file; only a half-written temporary file is removed on failure.


---

<!-- https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-errors.html -->

# 12.10. Error propagation

Morloc Manual > Build Architecture | https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-errors.html | prev: https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-streaming.md | next: https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-collect.md

> A failure can start in any language, several calls deep, in a different process from the code that should handle it. This section specifies the two kinds of failure the runtime distinguishes, how a recoverable failure travels back through pools as an error packet gathering a traceback, how `@try` turns it into a value, and how a failure of the runtime itself ends a run.

**Two kinds of failure.**

| Kind | Examples | Caught by `@try` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Recoverable | An exception raised by user code in any language; `@throw` in Morloc; a Rust panic in user code. | Yes |
| Infrastructure | A pool that crashed or was killed; a broken connection; an internal error (panic) in the runtime. | No |

A recoverable failure means the computation went wrong; the program can decide what to do. An infrastructure failure means the system that runs the program went wrong, so no Morloc code can be trusted to handle it.

**Recoverable failures.** Each generated function catches a failure that escapes it, appends one traceback line, and raises it again:

```
  at <function> [<language>] (mid=<index>, <file>:<line>:<column>)
```

Anonymous functions are named `_`. At the edge of a pool, the failure becomes an error packet (status 1, text payload; [Packet protocol](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-packets.md)) carrying the message and the lines so far. The calling pool’s stub reads the error packet and raises it as a native failure in its own language, whose functions then add their lines. So the traceback grows across every pool the failure crosses, innermost call first:

```
nope
  at _ [py] (mid=2366, t.loc:12:23)
  at _ [cpp] (mid=2364, t.loc:12:17)
  at chain [cpp] (mid=4, t.loc:1:34)
```

A program built with `morloc make --debug` also records each active frame’s arguments when a failure passes through it, and adds them to the message.

**`@try`.** `@try e` evaluates `e`. If it completes, the result is `Ok v`; if a recoverable failure escapes it, the result is `Err msg`, where `msg` is the message with the traceback gathered so far. A failure is caught the same way whichever language raised it.

**At the nexus.** A failure that reaches the nexus ends a one-shot run with `Error: run failed`, the message and its traceback on standard error, and exit status 1. A command whose result is a variant whose arm is named `Err` is treated the same way: the value is printed on standard error and the run exits 1, so a failing command fails in a shell pipeline even though it returned a value. A daemon answers the request as failed and keeps serving.

**Infrastructure failures.** A pool that loses a pool it called, or whose runtime breaks one of its own invariants, does not answer with an error packet: it ends its own worker. Its caller then sees a closed connection, which is itself an infrastructure failure, so the failure travels to the nexus whatever code lies between, and no `@try` along the way can catch it. The nexus reports which pool died and how, ends the run with status 1 (70 if the nexus itself panicked; [Process lifecycle](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-lifecycle.md)), and removes the run’s processes and shared memory. A daemon fails the request and restarts its pools. A process that dies prints its own diagnostics to the standard error it shares with the nexus, so they reach the user directly.

**Closed output.** Writing to a standard output that the reader has closed (as with `| head`) is neither: the pool answers with status 2, and the nexus ends the run with status 141, as a native program would.


---

<!-- https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-collect.html -->

# 12.11. Collect, fold, parse and render

Morloc Manual > Build Architecture | https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-collect.html | prev: https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-errors.md | next: https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-runs.md

> A command’s docstring can attach data-flow directives to it: `@parse` reads an argument from a file in a foreign format, `@collect` streams a command’s output instead of returning it whole, and output actions (`@render`, `@with`, with `@fold`) turn that output into other results, each written to its own destination. The chapters on [Arguments](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/clis/arguments.md), [Streaming output with `@collect`](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/clis/streaming-output.md) and [Output actions](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/clis/output-actions.md) show how to use them; this section specifies where each step runs, what is held in memory, and how several outputs are produced from one run.

**Everything is compiled into ordinary commands.** The compiler lowers each directive into Morloc code and, where needed, into extra commands in the manifest that the user never names: a **parse entry** per command with parsed arguments, an **action entry** per output action, and a **replay entry** per action for multi-output runs. The nexus only chooses which entries to run and where their output goes; all user-level work (parsing, folding, formatting) runs in pools.

**`@parse`.** An argument declares named formats, each with file extensions. The nexus picks a format by looking only at the argument’s text, never the file’s contents:

1.  A `name:` prefix selects that format (`morloc:` reads an ordinary Morloc value).
2.  Otherwise the longest matching extension wins, ignoring case.
3.  Otherwise the argument is read as an ordinary value. `-` is standard input, which at most one argument may claim.

The parse entry then calls the format’s handler in a pool with the path. A plain argument’s handler returns the value, and every such argument is parsed before the command body starts. An `IStream` argument’s handler feeds batches to the command as it runs. An `IFile` argument is first written to a stream file in a temporary **stage** directory and opened from there. A handler’s failure names the argument, format and path, and ends the run with status 1.

**`@collect`.** `@collect producer` gives the producer a sink and streams whatever it passes to the sink to the command’s output, batch by batch. The batches travel through shared memory to the nexus, which writes each in the requested format as it arrives. Nothing is gathered: memory use does not grow with the output.

**Output actions** consume what the command collects. Each runs as its own entry, a copy of the command whose sink is replaced:

| Kind | Sink, and what the handler receives |
| --- | --- |
| gather | Writes every batch to a temporary stream file. The handler receives the whole list, or an `IFile` handle to read it at random without loading it. |
| `@stream` | Calls the handler on each batch inside the sink. Memory stays constant. |
| `@fold` | Folds each batch into an accumulator with `@fold`, starting from `@init`. Each thread keeps its own accumulator; at the end they are merged with `@combine` in the order the threads first folded, and the handler receives the result. |

A `@render` handler returns bytes (`Str`, `[Str]`, `Vector U8` or a list of `Vector U8`), which are written verbatim, ignoring `-f`. A `@with` handler returns a typed value, which is written in the `-f` format.

**One output.** When only standard output is wanted, the nexus runs the action’s entry directly (or the command itself) and writes its result.

**Several outputs.** When an action writes to a file, or a command has more than one action, the run is **staged**:

![Diagram](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/static/img/mermaid-f89fe193bc4902f592b5ac41682092b7.svg)

1.  A stage process runs the command once and saves its value, its collected stream and its arguments as packet files. If standard output wants the command’s own output, the stage also writes it there as it runs.
2.  Each action is replayed in its own process on the saved output, writing to a temporary file beside its target.
3.  Only when every process has succeeded are the temporary files renamed into place. A failure removes them and ends the run with the failing process’s status, so a named output is either complete or untouched.

The command body runs once however many outputs are requested, so a slow or effectful command is never repeated per output. Output formats are checked against every destination before anything runs, and conflicting destinations (two claims on standard output, two outputs to one file) are a usage error with status 2.


---

<!-- https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-runs.html -->

# 12.12. Logs and result caching

Morloc Manual > Build Architecture | https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-runs.html | prev: https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-collect.md | next: https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/index.md

> A run can leave two kinds of state behind it, both opt-in: a **log directory** recording what the run did, and a **result cache** that lets a later run skip a call it has already made. Both outlive the run, unlike the private run directory of [Process lifecycle](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-lifecycle.md), which is always removed. This section specifies how each is activated, its layout and formats, and what holds when several runs share them.

## 12.12.1. Log directory

`--log-dir DIR` (or `MORLOC_LOG_DIR`) gives each run its own directory, `DIR/<run id>/`, where the run id is the start time in UTC plus eight random hex digits (`20261009T143000Z-1a2b3c4d`). A Morloc program started by another program’s pool inherits the outer run’s directory, so a nested pipeline logs into one place. The directory is created on first write and never removed.

| File | Contents |
| --- | --- |
| `log` | Run-scope lines: the prologue, the epilogue, and the benchmark summary. |
| `<label>/log` | Start, pass and fail lines for calls in a labeled group. |
| `summary.json` | Written once, at exit, by atomic rename (below). |
| `debug/inputs/<hash>.pkt` | Programs built with `--debug` only: the arguments of each frame a failure passed through, as self-contained voidstar packets. |

`summary.json` holds `status` (`ok` or `fail`), `exit_code`, `command`, `run_id`, `started_at` and `finished_at` (RFC 3339), `wall_ms`, `morloc_version` and `error` (null on success). Because it appears only by rename, a script may wait for the file to exist and then read it whole. `--summary FILE` writes the same object to a chosen path instead.

**Log lines** come from templates in the program’s configuration, with placeholders such as `{name}`, `{run_id}`, `{runtime}`, `{exit_code}` and `{error}`. Placeholders known at build time are filled in by the compiler; the rest by the nexus as the line is written. Every line goes to standard error (colored only on a terminal) and to the matching log file. There are no levels; `--quiet` suppresses all of them. At exit the nexus writes the benchmark summary (count, mean, min, max, total and standard deviation per labeled function, from one timing record per successful call), then the epilogue, then `summary.json`.

## 12.12.2. Result cache

A labeled group configured with `cache: true` has its calls cached. The compiler wraps each such call: compute a key, return the stored result on a hit, otherwise run the call and store its result. Only successful results are stored. The key, the layout of entries and the rules that let many runs share them are specified in [Caching](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/ecosystem-architecture/eco-caching.md).


---

<!-- https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/ -->

# 13. Compiler Architecture

Morloc Manual | https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/ | prev: https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-runs.md | next: https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-pipeline.md

This chapter specifies how the compiler turns Morloc source into the artifacts described in [Build Architecture](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/index.md). It begins with a map of the pipeline. It then follows a program through it: parsing and module loading, typechecking, effects, term sharing, realization, segmentation into pools, serialization, ownership and code generation. It ends with how the manifest’s command interface is derived, how a new language is brought into Morloc, and the API of the runtime library, which is the contract every language binding is written against.


---

<!-- https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-pipeline.html -->

# 13.1. Pipeline overview

Morloc Manual > Compiler Architecture | https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-pipeline.html | prev: https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/index.md | next: https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-parsing.md

> The compiler is a sequence of passes over three kinds of program representation: a graph of modules, a set of typed expression trees (one per exported function), and per-language trees of callable units that become pool source. This section lists the passes in order and states what each consumes, produces and guarantees to the passes after it. It is the map for the rest of the chapter.

**Three phases.** The **frontend** reads source into a module graph, dissolves it into one expression tree per export, and typechecks those trees with **general** types: types that name no language. The **middle** chooses, for every call, which implementation runs and in which language. The **backend** lowers each realized tree into **manifolds**: the compiler’s unit of generated function, one per call site that needs a function of its own. It cuts the manifolds into per-language pools, adds serialization where values cross, and prints source text.

![Diagram](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/static/img/mermaid-4e24c3a394e8c57503e628c86c1c95db.svg)

**The passes.** Each pass may assume what the passes before it established. A pass that receives input violating one of these guarantees stops with an internal compiler error; no pass repairs its input.

| Pass | Produces | Guarantees after it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Lex and parse ([Parsing and module loading](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-parsing.md)) | One syntax tree per source file | Layout is explicit; sugar (`do`, holes, string interpolation) is desugared to core expressions. |
| Load modules ([Parsing and module loading](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-parsing.md)) | A directed acyclic graph of modules, edges labeled by import lists | Every import names a loaded module and only names that module exports. |
| Resolve names and link ([Parsing and module loading](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-parsing.md)) | Global tables of signatures, implementations, types and instances | Every name refers to exactly one declaration; local binders are unique program-wide; the several definitions of one term are merged. |
| One tree per export | An expression tree per exported function, with declarations inlined at their uses | The module graph is gone; trees carry every candidate implementation of each term. |
| Typecheck and specialize ([Type system](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-types.md)) | Trees annotated with general types | Every node has a general type; a polymorphic definition is elaborated once per type it is used at. |
| Value checks and term sharing ([Term sharing and inlining](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-sharing.md)) | Trees with sharing made explicit | Alternative implementations do not provably contradict; a discarded `Try` is rejected; each named value is computed once. |
| Realize ([Realization](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-realization.md)) | Pure trees, and realized trees with one implementation and language per node | Every call has exactly one implementation. A tree with no foreign call is pure and is evaluated by the nexus. |
| Manifest ([Interface generation](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-interface.md)) | The command schema for every export | Each concrete export becomes a command; a generic export is skipped with a warning. |
| Express manifolds ([Segmentation and cross-language calls](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-calls.md)) | Per-language manifold trees with concrete types | Every node has its concrete type in its language; applied lambdas are reduced. |
| Insert effect boundaries ([Effects](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-effects.md)) | Trees with every suspension and force explicit | The number of times each suspension runs is fixed; no later pass changes it. |
| Segment into pools ([Segmentation and cross-language calls](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-calls.md)) | One set of manifolds per language | No manifold calls across a language except through a foreign-call node. |
| Serialize ([Serialization](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-serialization.md)) | Manifolds with pack and unpack at every crossing | Every crossing value has a wire form both sides agree on. |
| Emit pool source ([Code generation](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-codegen.md), [Ownership](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-ownership.md)) | Source text of each pool | Each read of a value in C++ and Rust is a borrow, copy or move. |
| Build | The program directory of [Compilation artifacts](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-artifacts.md) | Pools are compiled, and the manifest records each pool’s source fingerprint. |

**General and concrete types.** The frontend works only with general types, so a program typechecks before any language is chosen. Concrete types, the native types a value has in one language, enter after realization. Keeping them apart is what lets one signature have implementations in several languages and lets the compiler choose among them late ([Type system](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-types.md), [Realization](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-realization.md)).

**Trees, not a graph.** After the frontend each export is its own tree, and a definition used in several places appears at each of them. Done naively, this duplicates terms exponentially in nesting depth. Term sharing and the rule that a definition is elaborated once per type keep the output proportional to the source ([Term sharing and inlining](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-sharing.md)).

**What runs where.** Realization divides the program. A pure tree never reaches a pool: the nexus evaluates it directly. A realized tree becomes manifolds, and segmentation places each manifold in the pool of its language. The call from the nexus enters a pool at the manifold of the export, and calls between pools go through generated stubs ([Segmentation and cross-language calls](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-calls.md)).

**Inspecting the pipeline.** `morloc dump` prints the program after parsing. `morloc typecheck` runs the frontend and prints each export’s general type; with `--realize` it also runs realization. Neither command builds pools.


---

<!-- https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-parsing.html -->

# 13.2. Parsing and module loading

Morloc Manual > Compiler Architecture | https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-parsing.html | prev: https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-pipeline.md | next: https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-types.md

> The first frontend passes turn source text into a graph of modules in which every name refers to exactly one declaration. This section specifies how text becomes tokens, how indentation becomes explicit block structure, how sugar is removed, where docstrings attach, how imports are found and loaded, and how names, namespaces, exports and the many definitions of one term are resolved. Its output is the input of the type checker ([Type system](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-types.md)).

**Tokens.** A token starting `--` opens a line comment and `{-` …​ `-}` a block comment; block comments nest. Two comment forms are kept: `--'` lines are docstrings and `--*` lines name export groups. The case of a name’s first character fixes its class: lowercase or `_` for terms and type variables, uppercase for types, constructors, classes and kinds. Keywords cannot be names. A few tokens depend on the whitespace around them, so the lexer decides them rather than the grammar:

| Written | Token |
| --- | --- |
| `.f r`, `.[i] xs` | A `.` after whitespace or a delimiter opens a getter pattern; a `.` written directly against the previous token continues a getter chain (`.a.b`). |
| `x@p` | No whitespace on either side: `x` is bound to the whole of `p`. |
| `@name` | After whitespace or a delimiter: an intrinsic. |
| `-3` | A `-` against a digit, in operand position, is part of the literal. |
| `n.f` | One qualified name: `f` reached through the namespace `n`. If `n` is not a namespace of the module, this is an error, which catches a composition written without spaces. |

**Layout.** Indentation is turned into explicit structure before parsing, as virtual `{`, `;` and `}` tokens, so the grammar itself is free of indentation. A block opens after `where`, `let` and `do`, and around a module body. The column of the block’s first token is its indentation: a later line starting at that column begins a new item, one starting left of it closes the block. A `let` block also closes at `in`. An explicit `{` directly after the keyword switches the block to braces and semicolons, and inside parentheses and brackets indentation is not tracked. One exception keeps record literals usable after `do`: `{` followed by a lowercase name and `=` is a record literal, since no statement begins with `name =`.

**Grammar and desugaring.** The parser reads the token stream into a concrete syntax tree that keeps source spans for diagnostics. Desugaring then lowers it to a small core of expressions and declarations, each node with a unique index that later passes use to attach types, source locations and metadata:

| Written | Core form |
| --- | --- |
| A file with no `module` header | A module named `main` holding every declaration. |
| Lowercase variables in a signature | Universally quantified over the whole signature. |
| `"x = #{e}"` | A text pattern applied to the interpolated expressions. |
| `do` blocks | Sequenced binds ([Effects](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-effects.md)). |
| `a + b * c` | Kept as a flat chain until imports are resolved (below). |

Operator chains wait because a fixity declaration travels with its operator: the precedence of `*` in one module may be declared in a module it imports. Once imports are resolved, each chain is re-associated using the fixities in scope in its module, plus the built-in defaults ([Infix operators](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/types/infix-operators.md)).

**Docstrings.** The lexer removes `--'` lines and keys each consecutive run by the position of the token that follows it; the parser attaches the run to the declaration starting there. A docstring may describe a module header, a signature (the term, never its return type), one argument type inside a signature, a `source` list item, a `type`, `newtype` or `record` declaration, or a record field. A line starting `@keyword` is a directive, any other line is prose; an unknown directive is kept as prose with a warning. A docstring on a `type` alias is inherited by every argument written with that alias, and the nearest docstring wins: one written on the argument, then the alias named there, then the next alias down its chain. A term’s docstrings are never inherited through `bar = foo`. How docstrings become a command-line interface is [Interface generation](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-interface.md); the user’s view is [Docstrings](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/clis/docstrings.md).

**Module graph.** Each `module` keyword starts a module, which runs to the next `module` keyword or the end of the file. Loading begins with the entry file and repeats: for every import edge whose target is not yet loaded, find the target’s file, parse it, and add its modules and edges. The result is a directed graph of modules, edges labeled by import lists. A module that imports itself, or any import cycle, is a load error. Every module belongs to a **package**: the program, rooted at the entry file’s directory, or an installed module reached by a dotless import, rooted at its own directory.

| Import | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `import m` | The installed module `m`, and every term it exports. A missing module is installed first when the build allows it ([Module resolution](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/ecosystem-architecture/eco-modules.md)). |
| `import .a.b` | The local module `a/b.loc` or `a/b/main.loc`, under the root of the importing module’s package, so a package’s own imports mean the same wherever it is installed. In a package `p` other than the program, the module is `p.a.b`. |
| `import m (f, g as h, T)` | Only the listed items, optionally renamed. Listing an item `m` does not export is a load error, and a class method cannot be listed by name: import its class. |
| `import m as n` | Every term arrives as `n.f`; bare `f` is not in scope. |

An anonymous module (`module (*)` with no name) takes its name from the import that reaches it.

**Exports.** `module m (a, b)` exports exactly `a` and `b`, and exporting a name the module does not define is a load error. `module m ()` exports no terms. `module m (**)**` **exports every term defined in the module, and a term imported into a module counts as defined there, so a module that imports several others and exports `(`**`)` is their union. Export groups (`--*`) only organize the command-line help ([Interface generation](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-interface.md)).

**Name resolution.** After import resolution, every name in scope in a module maps to the declaration it came from. Terms are linked across modules by these maps. Type names are resolved where they are written: a type name in a signature keeps the meaning it has in the module that wrote the signature, and importing the term does not rebind it in the importer. Several types of one name may therefore coexist in a program, each bound to its own declaration; nothing resolves a type by its spelling in a global scope. An undeclared type name is a load error, as is importing a type and declaring the same name. Base type names such as `Int` and `Str` are ordinary declarations, so a program may supply its own prelude. Finally, every local binder (a lambda parameter, a `let` or `where` binding) is renamed to a name unique in the whole program, because later passes copy a definition’s body to each of its uses and a copied body must not capture a binder at the use site.

****One term, many definitions.** A signature \`f**

T\` declares one term with general type `T`. Every definition of `f` and every sourced function named `f` in scope is an implementation of that term, and a second definition adds an alternative rather than shadowing the first; which alternative runs is chosen by realization ([Realization](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-realization.md), [One term may have many definitions](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/types/term-polymorphism.md)). The rules that decide which term a signature or definition belongs to:

| Situation | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Two signatures for one name in one scope | Error, even when the types are equal. A `where` block is its own scope. |
| `f = e` with no signature for `f` in the module | One more implementation of the `f` in scope. This is how a language module adds implementations to a language-neutral module. |
| `f :: T` in a module that imports all of `m`, which exports `f` | A new term `f`. It replaces the imported one here and in every module that imports `f` from here; the imported implementations are dropped. |
| `f :: T` in a module that imports `f` by name | Error; import it under another name instead. |

When one term reaches a module along several import paths, its implementations are merged into one set; two declarations whose general types differ are an error. Instances of one class at one type are merged the same way, their implementations joined as alternatives ([Type system](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-types.md)).

**Trees per export.** Once every name is resolved and every declaration is merged, the graph is dissolved. Each exported term becomes one expression tree, in which every reference to a term carries the term’s full set of implementations. These trees are what the type checker sees.


---

<!-- https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-types.html -->

# 13.3. Type system

Morloc Manual > Compiler Architecture | https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-types.html | prev: https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-parsing.md | next: https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-effects.md

> Morloc checks a program against **general** types, which name no language, and only later gives each value a **concrete** type in the language that holds it. This section specifies the checker: bidirectional inference with an ordered context, how polymorphism is resolved before anything runs, typeclass instance selection, kinds and the side solvers for type-level naturals, strings, lists, sets and rows, aliases and newtypes, and type equality. It ends with how a general type becomes a concrete one. Effects are in [Effects](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-effects.md); choosing the language of each call is [Realization](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-realization.md).

****Two layers of types.** A signature such as \`sum**

\[Int\] → Int\` is general: it says what the function means, in every language at once. A **native form** (`type L ⇒ …​`) says how one language spells a general type. The checker reasons only about general types. Concrete types are derived after realization has placed every call in a language, by translating the general type through that language’s native forms.

![Diagram](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/static/img/mermaid-2fc639fd546d93ca8785d801c4084eba.svg)

**Bidirectional checking.** The checker follows the ordered-context design of Dunfield and Krishnaswami. Each term is either **checked** against a type it is expected to have (an argument, an annotated body, a definition with a signature) or has its type **synthesized** from its parts (a variable, an application). The context is an ordered list of universally bound variables, unsolved **existential** variables, solved existentials and scope markers; order fixes which existential may mention which variable, so a solution can never escape the scope of a variable it uses. Instantiating a polymorphic type creates fresh existentials, and checking against one binds its variables in the context. Where an expected type meets a synthesized one, the checker requires the synthesized type to be a subtype. An unsolved existential can already carry partial knowledge, such as the record fields or tuple positions read from it, and that knowledge is checked when it is solved.

**Subtyping is narrow.** It does three things and nothing else: it relates a polymorphic type to its instances; it lets `T` flow into `?T`, the only value coercion in the language ([Optional types](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/features/optionals.md)); and it lets a type with a known dimension flow into the same type with that dimension omitted, so `Vector 3 Real` is accepted where `Vector Real` is expected. `Int` is not a subtype of `Real`. Dimensions in the same slot must be equal after reduction.

**Polymorphism.** A lowercase variable in a signature is universally quantified over the whole signature, and each use of the term instantiates it afresh. Every polymorphic use is resolved to concrete types at compile time: no value crosses a language boundary at a type that still holds a variable. To get there, a definition is typed at each type it is used at: either a copy of its body is checked at each use or, when it has a signature, the body is checked once against the signature and elaborated once per distinct type of use. Recursion at a different type than the one being elaborated (polymorphic recursion) has no finite set of elaborations and is rejected.
