A variable that nothing determines, where a native representation needs it, is an error at the term where it occurs and names the variable; a variable no representation needs, such as a phantom parameter, is not.

**Typeclasses.** A class declares method signatures; each method name belongs to one class. A method used at type `T` runs an implementation of the instance for `T`, and that instance’s implementations are all those given for it, in any language and any module: they are alternatives, like the several definitions of one term ([Parsing and module loading](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-parsing.md)). Selection works on general types. The candidates are the instances whose head the use-site type is an instance of; the most specific one is kept. If the candidates have no unique most specific head (two heads overlap and neither specializes the other), the use is rejected as ambiguous. An instance on a transparent `type` alias is rejected, since an alias is the same type as its expansion and would collide with its expansion’s instance. Instances never type a record literal: a literal whose type would come only from the instance a method resolves to is an error at the literal. See [Overload terms with typeclasses](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/types/typeclasses.md).

**Kinds.** A type parameter has kind `Type` unless declared otherwise (`(n :: Nat)`). The other kinds are `Nat`, `Str`, `Rec`, `List` and `Set`; values of these kinds exist only in the type system and are erased before anything runs. An alias parameter that fills only slots of one non-`Type` kind takes that kind. In a signature, a binder on an argument ties the argument’s value to a type-level variable: `n@Int` binds a `Nat`, `x@Str` a `Str`, `xs@[Str]` a `List`. See [The kind system](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/types/kinds.md) and [Tensors](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/types/tensors.md).

**Side solvers.** Equations between type-level expressions of a non-`Type` kind are handed to a solver for that kind. An equation a solver cannot decide yet is deferred and retried as variables are solved.

| Kind | What the solver decides |
| --- | --- |
| `Nat` | `+`, `-`, `*` and `/` (integer division) reduce when the operands are ground; expressions with variables are kept in a sum-of-products normal form. Two dimensions that reduce to different numbers are a type error. An equation still open when inference ends, such as `n + m = 4`, is accepted when it has a solution in the naturals, since dimensions are erased and the variables need no value; one with no solution is an error at the term that produced it. |
| `Rec` | Rows: labeled fields with row variables standing for unknown blocks of fields. Fields are matched by label, a row variable takes what is left, and a match with more than one solution is deferred. |
| `Str` | Literals only: two literals, or concatenations folding to literals, are compared. A free variable is solved by ordinary assignment, never by solving a word equation. |
| `List` | Ordered lists of strings. Ground prefixes and suffixes are stripped; a single variable against a ground remainder is solved; two variables defer. |
| `Set` | Unordered sets of strings, compared in a canonical sorted form. Union, intersection and difference reduce on ground operands. |

**Aliases.** A `type` alias is the same type as its expansion, in every position. Two aliases with one expansion are the same type. The checker keeps alias names in the types it reports, so diagnostics name the alias, but it unfolds an alias head wherever two types are compared or decomposed, so no judgment depends on whether an alias was written. An alias must be applied to all of its `Type` parameters, every parameter must appear in its body, and its body may name a type of any kind. A recursive alias is legal only when it is regular (the alias recurs at its own parameters) and every recursive occurrence sits under `?` or `[ ]`, as in `type T a = (a, ?(T a))`. An alias owns no instances and no native forms; it shares those of its expansion.

**Newtypes.** `newtype N = T` makes a new type that is never equal to `T` and crosses language boundaries in the form of `T`. It owns its instances and native forms. Values move between `N` and `T` only by explicit conversion through the `Packable` class: `unpack` comes with every newtype that has a representation, and `pack` with `deriving (Packable)`, which requires every parameter of `N` to be determined by `T`. A parameter of a newtype need not appear in its representation (`newtype Buffer (n :: Nat) a = List a`), which is how a dimension is added to an existing type. See [Naming a type: `type` and `newtype`](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/types/newtype.md) and [Serializing custom types with `Packable`](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/types/packable.md).

**Type equality.** Two types are equal when, with every alias unfolded, they are the same constructors applied to equal arguments, up to renaming of bound variables. Under a recursive alias the unfoldings are infinite, so equality is coinductive: a pair met again while it is being compared holds. A type name denotes its declaration, not its spelling, so two types of one name from different modules are different types. A newtype is equal only to itself. Ground `Nat` expressions are equal when they reduce to the same number.

**From general to concrete.** The concrete type of a value in language `L` is its general type translated through ``L’s native forms. A native form is a template over the type’s parameters: `type Cpp ⇒ List a = "std::vector<$1>" a`` spells `[Int]` by substituting the C++ spelling of `Int` for `$1`. The form text is opaque to Morloc and is checked only by the language’s own compiler or interpreter. Translation walks the type from the outside in. A head with a native form in `L` uses it; an alias with none unfolds one step and retries; a newtype with none uses its representation’s form; a `record` takes its field names and types from the general declaration and only its container from `record L ⇒ R = "name"`; a `data` type with no form is generated under its own name. How these concrete types reach generated code is [Realization](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-realization.md) and [Native type mappings](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/features/foreign-functions.md#mapping-native-types).


---

<!-- https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-effects.html -->

# 13.4. Effects

Morloc Manual > Compiler Architecture | https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-effects.html | prev: https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-types.md | next: https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-sharing.md

> An effectful type `<E> T` denotes a suspended computation: a value that, when run, may perform the effects in `E` and yields a `T`. This section specifies what the type checker requires of suspensions, when one is run, and how code generation turns them into closures of no arguments. It also covers how they are reconciled at every point where a value meets a calling convention that has no suspensions, so that each computation runs exactly as often, and in the order, the program says, in every language. The user-facing description is in [Effects and delayed evaluation](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/features/effects.md).

**A suspension is a value.** `<E> T` and `T` are different types, and no pass erases, strips or reinterprets the effect layer. The model is call-by-push-value: a suspension is a thunk, and the only way from `<E> T` to `T` is to run it. Holding, passing, returning, projecting or storing a suspension in a record, list or optional runs nothing. Every run runs the computation again. The compiler never shares, hoists, memoizes, duplicates or drops a run. This is the one place where morloc’s freedom to reorder and share work stops ([Term sharing and inlining](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-sharing.md)).

**Effect labels are tags.** The compiler gives a label no operational meaning. It propagates labels and checks that they are covered. What `IO` or `Rand` permits is decided by the library that declares it. Effects come from the signatures of sourced functions. Such a row is the author’s claim, which the compiler takes as given because it cannot look inside foreign code. Every other row is inferred by composition and checked against the signature that declares it.

**Typing.** Rows enter the bidirectional checker ([Type system](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-types.md)) through subtyping:

| Rule | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Inclusion | `<E1> T1 <: <E2> T2` when `E1` is a subset of `E2` and `T1 <: T2`. Label order is irrelevant and duplicates collapse. Widening is accepted and narrowing is rejected. |
| No coercion | A `T` never fills an `<E> T` slot, and an `<E> T` never fills a `T` slot. `do v` is the only lift, and it has type `<> T`, which fits any row. |
| Body fits signature | The effects a definition’s body runs must be a subset of the row in its signature. Declaring more than the body runs is legal. |
| Layers stay apart | `<E> (<E'> T)` is two suspensions, never `<E,E'> T`. |
| Row variables | A row may end in a variable standing for unknown further labels, so combinators can thread a callback’s effects into their result. An unconstrained row variable is `<>` at ground. |

**Building and running.** A `do` block builds one suspension from its statements. Only a bind runs a suspension: `x ← t`, or a bare statement `t`. Application, `let`, projection, passing and returning run nothing. `!e` is sugar for a bind inserted above the statement that contains it, with a fresh name in its place. The front end hoists every `!` into an explicit bind and desugars each block into nested binds, so later passes see only two operations: **suspend** (build a thunk around an expression) and **force** (run a thunk once). A force applied directly to a suspend cancels.

**Evaluation order.** Pure work has no order: the compiler may move, parallelize or reorder it, including the arguments of one call. The only order the compiler must keep is the order of effect statements in a `do` block. A pure `let` in a block is never computed before an effect statement written above it. A pure argument is evaluated once, at the application. When a suspension is built from a call whose arguments still need work, the arguments are computed outside it and the suspension captures their values, so a second run repeats the call and nothing else.

**Failure is not an effect.** A fallible operation returns `Try e a`, an ordinary data type. `@throw` abandons the computation and carries no row. `@try :: <e> a → <e> (Try Str a)` catches every recoverable failure that escapes its argument, whichever language raised it, and passes the row through unchanged. Internal errors and interrupts bypass it. See [Failure is not an effect](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/features/effects.md#failure-is-not-an-effect).

**Effect boundaries.** After realization and segmentation ([Realization](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-realization.md), [Segmentation and cross-language calls](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-calls.md)), every position in a pool’s tree sits under a boundary that dictates a calling convention: a plain value or the suspension itself. A boundary pass compares each position’s declared type with its boundary and inserts a force or a suspend wherever they differ by a layer:

| Boundary | Expects | Reconciliation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Return of a command | plain | The root of a command whose result is `<E> T` is forced once, so the wire carries the `T` the caller asked for. |
| Argument of a command | suspension | The caller of a program holds values, not thunks. An argument declared `<E> T` arrives as a `T`, and each reference to it becomes a suspension with a constant result. |
| Sourced call | suspension | Foreign functions are eager. When a source is declared to return `<E> T`, the host call becomes the body of a suspension, so running the suspension calls the host function. |
| Callback into a host | plain | A morloc function handed to a host at an `A → <E> C` slot is wrapped as `\a → force (g a)`, because the host calls it and expects the effect to happen. |
| Host function into morloc | suspension | A host function received at that type is wrapped to build the suspension the type promises. |
| Cross-pool call, callee side | plain | The callee’s entry point runs one layer, and the result travels over the wire. |
| Cross-pool call, caller side | suspension | The caller holds the remote call as a suspension, so forcing it makes the call. |
| Wire serializer | either | A suspension passed as data crosses as a closure that calls back to its home pool once per run ([Serialization](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-serialization.md)). |

Host conversion follows the declared type to any depth: function arguments (contravariantly), results, record fields, tuple and list elements, optionals, and packable types. Under a type variable of the source’s signature the host holds the value opaquely, so nothing there is converted. A sourced `map :: (a → b) → f a → f b` used at `b = <IO> C` builds suspensions and does not run them. A value that cannot be rebuilt at its type is refused at build time with an error. After boundaries are placed, no later pass adds or removes a force. Passes may move and rename code, but the number of runs on every path is fixed.

**Lowering.** A suspend becomes a closure of no arguments. Its captured variables are the expression’s free variables, copied into the closure when it is built. A force becomes a call of that closure with no arguments. A suspension therefore shares every code path a closure already has. It can be stored in an aggregate, captured, passed to a foreign function as a callable, and sent across pools ([Code generation](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-codegen.md)). An intrinsic whose result is declared as a suspension (`@save`, `@try` and the like) is the eager runtime call. Forcing it calls it, and holding it builds a closure that makes the call.

![Diagram](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/static/img/mermaid-11239ca961d93fb6a491a83935d861f2.svg)


---

<!-- https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-sharing.html -->

# 13.5. Term sharing and inlining

Morloc Manual > Compiler Architecture | https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-sharing.html | prev: https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-effects.md | next: https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-realization.md

> The compiler expands each named term at every place it is used, so that each use can be realized on its own, in its own language. Done naively, that expansion makes generated code, and type checking, grow exponentially with the depth of the program’s call graph. This section specifies how the compiler keeps both proportional to the source: shared specializations for functions, let-sharing for data values, shared closures for lambdas in pools, and static-argument specialization for recursive helpers. Each one preserves the evaluation semantics of [Effects](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-effects.md).

**Inline by name.** A morloc term may have several implementations in different languages, and realization chooses one for each call ([Realization](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-realization.md)). So the front end does not compile a definition once and call it. It substitutes the definition at every name that refers to it, with fresh indices, and each copy is realized independently. A `where` binding is treated the same way as a top-level definition.

**Why that explodes.** If each level of a definition names the one below it twice, `d` levels of expansion produce `2^d` copies:

```morloc
f0 x = g x
f1 x = f0 x + f0 (x + 1)
f2 x = f1 x + f1 (x + 1)
-- ... f_d has 2^d copies of f0, and type checking pays the same exponent
```

The same thing happens with a value. `y = expensive x` named twice in `where` would be computed twice per copy. That costs time, and it would also violate the language’s evaluation rules: a pure argument is evaluated once, at the application, and a named value is computed at most once each time its scope is evaluated.

**Shared specializations.** A signed definition is checked once against its signature. Each use is then solved to a type, and that type, with the definition, forms a **key**. The definition is elaborated once per key, and every use at the same key gets that one elaboration, so checking cost follows the number of distinct keys, not the number of paths. When a use’s type is not fully solved, the definition or export that contains it is checked with every term expanded in place. An elaboration is either copied to each use or **shared**: emitted as a root of its own, which each use calls by name. Sharing turns copies into calls, so it is allowed only when that changes neither what the program computes nor how often it computes it:

| Condition | Why |
| --- | --- |
| A function of at least one argument, whose result is not a suspension | A shared root is called. A constant or a suspension would be evaluated per call instead of per use. |
| Every implementation takes all its arguments at once and is already a value | A function that does work before returning a function is evaluated once per command. As a root it would be evaluated once per call. |
| Fully solved key, no recursion out of the body | A recursion keeps its back-edges inside the copy that contains it. |
| Reads no top-level constant | Such a constant is computed once per command at the use. Inside a root it would be recomputed per call. |
| Larger than a small size threshold | Small bodies are cheaper to inline, and inlining them does not compound. |

Sourced implementations of a shared term stay at each use, so realization can still pick a foreign implementation per call site and fall back to the shared root.

**Let-sharing.** After type checking, the copies of a data-typed binding (a type with no function or suspension inside it) are merged within one evaluation of their scope and bound once, as a `let`, at the nearest point that every use passes through. The binding may be a parameterless `where`, a top-level constant, or a `let`. Placement has three rules:

-   A use in one arm of a conditional, in one implementation of a term, or in the argument of `@try` is served inside that arm. A value read only by a `@try` argument is computed inside it, so its failure becomes that ``@try’s `Err``. Uses in several exclusive arms are each served in their own arm.
-   A pure `let` in a `do` block is never placed above an effect statement written before it. An effectful `let`, a block’s discarded statement, and a pattern check’s guard are never moved.
-   A `where` binding nothing reads is never computed.

A top-level constant, or a value a definition computes without reading its parameters, is computed at most once per command, however many functions or recursion levels its copies came from. A value read by pools in several languages is computed once and passed to each ([Segmentation and cross-language calls](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-calls.md)).

**Beta-reduction.** Expansion leaves applied lambdas, `(\x → body) arg`, which code generation reduces before segmentation. Because arguments are strict, an argument is substituted into the body only when it is a value: evaluating it computes nothing. In a pool, even a value is substituted only when the parameter is used at most once, or when it is a scalar literal; otherwise it is bound once and shared. Any other argument is bound once by a `let` at the application, whatever its reference count, zero included, so its work happens exactly once and in the right place. When a substituted value is used once, the argument itself moves into the body and nothing is copied, which keeps a long chain of reductions linear.

**Lambdas: inlined or shared.** What happens to a lambda bound to a name and used more than once depends on where the code runs:

| Where | Rule |
| --- | --- |
| Pure nexus evaluation | A command with no language pool is evaluated by the nexus itself, which holds only data and cannot keep a function value. Every lambda is inlined at every use. A function computed by an expression is split into its strict parts, bound once, and a choice among function values that is substituted. A computation with no such form is rejected with an error asking for a language pool. |
| Pools | A lambda used once is reduced away. A lambda used more than once is kept as one native closure and each use calls it, so its body is emitted once. A function computed by an expression is split the same way when possible, and otherwise computed once into a closure that each use calls. |

**Static-argument specialization.** A recursive helper that receives a function and passes it unchanged to every recursive call would otherwise carry it as a closure value, which is heavier than a direct reference. Through a serial entry point the closure is a proxy that calls back into the pool once per application. When a call site passes a **closed** function (a sourced function, or a lambda with no free variables) at such a position, the helper gets its own copy with that function written in place and the parameter removed. The transformation is optional, so anything unrecognized is left alone: helpers whose back-edges do not all pass the parameter through, helpers carrying a label or cache configuration keyed to their own manifold, partial applications (which would be recomputed every iteration), and arguments that are not closed values. Copies are bounded: calls passing the same sourced function share one copy, a copy is never specialized again on a helper it copies, and each helper has a fixed maximum number of copies.

![Diagram](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/static/img/mermaid-127c9d4d37bd5f27a69da701c4a6b0db.svg)


---

<!-- https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-realization.html -->

# 13.6. Realization

Morloc Manual > Compiler Architecture | https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-realization.html | prev: https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-sharing.md | next: https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-calls.md

> A Morloc term may have several implementations: sourced functions in different languages, several in one language, and definitions written in Morloc itself. Realization chooses one implementation for every use of a term and one language for every node of each exported tree. It sits between typechecking and segmentation: its input is a typed tree in which each use of a term still carries all of its alternatives, and its output is a tree in which each node has exactly one implementation and one language, or no language at all when the nexus evaluates it. This section specifies the search space, the score being minimized, how ties are broken, and the placement rules that the score alone does not decide.

**What is chosen.** The user-facing view is in [One term may have many definitions](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/types/term-polymorphism.md): one name, many definitions. The author’s claim in declaring them under one name is that they compute the same value, so realization treats them as interchangeable and chooses among them on cost alone. A term defined in Morloc has no language of its own. Its body is realized wherever its uses need it, so one definition can run in Python at one call and in C++ at another. A shared value or specialization ([Term sharing and inlining](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-sharing.md)) is scored once and then realized once for each language its uses land in, each copy under its own name. The result is the same every time the same program is built by the same compiler.

**Search.** Realization is a two-pass dynamic program over each tree.

-   **Scoring**, bottom up, gives every node a table from language to the best score of its subtree when that node runs in that language. A sourced call has one entry, its own language. An application combines its head’s table with, for each argument, the cheapest way to have that argument in the head’s language. A node with several alternatives takes, per language, the cheapest alternative. Literals, containers and other language-free nodes take the languages their context offers.
-   **Collapse**, top down, gives the root its cheapest language and then gives each child the language that minimizes its own score plus the cost of the edge from its parent’s language. At a node with alternatives, the cheapest alternative from the parent’s language is kept and the rest are discarded.

Before scoring, applications of a literal lambda whose parameter is used at most once are reduced, so that a long point-free composition does not make the scorer revisit the same function arguments again and again.

**Cost.** A score counts crossings between pools, grouped by depth, then changes of language within one pool, then the sourced calls placed in each language, grouped by the language’s rank in a fixed preference order, then the number of sourced calls. Scores are added along the tree and compared part by part in that order: crossings from the greatest depth down, so one crossing at a greater depth outweighs any number at a smaller one; calls from the least preferred language upward.

| Part | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Crossing | An edge between two languages in different pools is one crossing, whatever values cross it. A value made in one pool, passed through a second and used in a third crosses twice. An edge between languages that share a pool, such as a guest language in its host’s pool ([Language onboarding](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-onboarding.md)), is a switch. |
| Depth | Code at the root of an exported function is at depth 0. A function or suspension passed to a sourced function, or to a shared specialization, is one deeper than the call, and the body of a recursive definition is one deeper than the call that enters it: either may run more than once per call. A function value passed to a definition in Morloc is counted where the body uses it. |
| Preference | The order is one table shipped with the compiler: compiled languages first, then interpreted ones, a language with no entry last. It decides only between placements that cross equally often at every depth. |
| Size | Fewer sourced calls wins, so a sourced implementation beats a Morloc definition that does the same work in the same languages by calling several. |

Code the nexus evaluates costs nothing, and starting a pool costs nothing, since pools start once per run.

**Ties.** Before cost, alternatives whose types differ are separated by type: the most specific instance whose type matches the use wins, and an instance on a nearer alias beats one on a farther alias. Two instances that both match with neither more specific are rejected as ambiguous. A node with no implementation of its own, such as a `let` or a container, keeps its parent’s language when its options tie. Two sources of one term in one language are refused before realization; two sources still tied after every part of the score are refused at build, naming both. Definitions in Morloc that tie are interchangeable, and a fixed one is used, so the choice never varies between builds.

**Checking the built placement.** Collapse is meant to build the placement scoring found cheapest. With verbosity, `morloc typecheck --realize` scores the built tree again with every node fixed to the language and implementation collapse chose, and lists any difference beside the placement. A node built in a language its table does not offer, such as a lambda built in its parent’s language around a body placed elsewhere, is priced as reaching its table from there.

**Placement rules.** Some placements are fixed rather than scored:

-   A sourced function runs in the language it is sourced from.
-   A lambda is built in its parent’s language; only its body chooses, and a call the body makes elsewhere is an ordinary crossing there.
-   A function value stored in a container, or passed directly to a sourced function, is homed in that container’s or host’s language, so the host receives a native callable ([Segmentation and cross-language calls](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-calls.md)).
-   A value bound by a `let` that holds a function and computes nothing to build, such as a lambda or a record of lambdas and suspensions, is built again in each language that uses it, so a use in another language calls its own copy rather than crossing back to the first. A bound function that is computed is built once, in its definition’s best language, and every use reaches it there.
-   A function that sourced code makes stays in its pool. The compiler follows where every function value was made through every construct and every call: a sourced call makes each function in its result, unless the source’s signature gives that position a type variable that one of its parameters also holds, in which case the result holds what the arguments held there; a function a source passes to a callback is made by that source; a lambda, a partial application or a suspension that Morloc builds is Morloc’s. A function inside a record field, a list element or a value of an alias type is followed like any other, and a function passed to a source returns its result where that source calls it, so a function another pool made cannot come back out of it. Every expression that holds or receives a function sourced code made, and the expression consuming it, is placed in that source’s language, and an argument computed from one is computed there so only its value crosses. A recursive function given one is built again for that language. A program that would carry one into another language, or serialize one, is refused at build.
-   When the call that makes such a function has sources in several languages, the source is chosen for the call alone; to have another make it, the program imports only the module that sources it in the language needed. A call given such a function may instead use its term’s source in the function’s language, when the term has one with the same call groups.
-   A language-free operation (building a list, tuple or record, applying a function value, a bracket access) runs in its context’s language only if that language can represent every type it works on. Otherwise it moves to the cheapest language that can.
-   A conversion between a newtype and its representation runs in a language where the newtype has no native form of its own, since only there is the conversion free.
-   Every node on a recursive cycle, from the recursive term down to each call that refers back to it, is placed in that term’s language or in a language that shares its pool. A cycle that crossed pools would nest one foreign call per level and park a worker in each pool per level, so its depth would be bounded by the number of workers rather than by memory. Kept in one pool, the cycle can become a loop ([Segmentation and cross-language calls](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-calls.md)), and the foreign calls its body makes are a bounded number per step. The outermost recursive term wins, so nested cycles agree.

**Nexus or pool.** A tree that calls nothing sourced gets no language. The nexus evaluates it directly, and the manifest marks its command `pure` ([Compilation artifacts](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-artifacts.md)). The nexus evaluator has no function values and cannot call a function by name, so two cases still need a pool. A term that calls itself is given one of the program’s pool languages, chosen by the same scoring; if the program imports no language at all, the build fails and asks for one. A shared specialization that takes a function argument is expanded at each of its nexus uses, while a first-order one is called by name. A language-free subtree used inside a realized tree runs in the pool of its context, exactly as if it had been written there.

**Result.** Every node of a realized tree carries one implementation and one language. The set of languages that appear is the set of pools the program needs, and every edge between two languages that do not share a pool is a cross-language call. Segmentation cuts the tree at exactly those edges ([Segmentation and cross-language calls](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-calls.md)).


---

<!-- https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-calls.html -->

# 13.7. Segmentation and cross-language calls

Morloc Manual > Compiler Architecture | https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-calls.html | prev: https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-realization.md | next: https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-serialization.md

> Realization leaves one tree per exported function with a language on every node ([Realization](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-realization.md)). This section specifies how such a tree becomes code that runs in several pools: the callable units the compiler builds (manifolds), how the tree is cut into one segment per language change, what the calling side and the receiving side of a cut do at run time, and how recursion and tail calls are compiled so that their depth is bounded only by the target language. The packet format and the worker model that carry these calls are in [Packet protocol](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-packets.md) and [Worker model](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-workers.md).

**Manifolds.** A **manifold** is the compiler’s unit of callable code: a function body with its parameters, identified by an integer index, its `mid`, that is unique across the whole program. Every exported command is a manifold, and the manifest records each command’s `mid` and pool ([Compilation artifacts](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-artifacts.md)). A manifold takes one of three forms:

| Form | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Full | A saturated call that produces a value. |
| Partial | A closure: some arguments are captured from the enclosing scope (its **context**), the rest are supplied when it is called. A closure of no remaining arguments is a suspension ([Effects](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-effects.md)). |
| Pass | An unapplied function handed to another function as a value; the receiver supplies every argument. |

**Parameterization** gives each manifold exactly the enclosing arguments its body uses: an argument a subtree never reads is not passed into it. This is what lets a subtree be moved into another process with a small, explicit interface.

**Expression.** Each realized tree is then rewritten into a per-language intermediate form. Every node gets its concrete type in its own language (aliases resolved, type parameters instantiated), and every edge where a child’s language differs from its parent’s is marked as a call interface naming the target language, the result type as the caller sees it, and the arguments that cross. Two languages that share a pool, such as a guest language in its host’s pool, get no interface: their call is an ordinary in-process call.

**Segmentation.** The tree is cut at every call interface. The subtree below a cut becomes the body of a new top-level manifold in the target language, under the `mid` its caller will name; in the caller, the subtree is replaced by a call stub. Cutting recurses, so a subtree can itself contain cuts back into the caller’s language. A pool is then the set of segments of one language, and a program needs one pool per language that owns a segment.

For example, with `inc` sourced from Python and `dbl` from C++, `foo x = inc (dbl (inc x))` realizes as below; the dashed edges are cuts:

![Diagram](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/static/img/mermaid-8b03d787a928659dde327216baefd924.svg)

The inner `inc` runs in the Python pool as a callback from C++: a segment is a subtree, so an argument whose producer lives in another language is reached by a call from the consumer, not computed beforehand by the caller.

**The calling side.** A stub serializes each argument to a data packet ([Serialization](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-serialization.md)), sends a call packet carrying the target `mid` to the target pool’s socket, and blocks until the single reply arrives. It then decodes the result into a native value and releases the reply’s shared memory. An argument that is already in serialized form, such as a command argument the nexus sent, is forwarded without being decoded. A call that the build configures to run as a cluster job is not sent to a local pool; it becomes a call packet that a pool on the cluster node reads from a file ([Packet protocol](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-packets.md)), and such calls have a dispatch table of their own.

**The receiving side.** Every pool has a dispatch table from `mid` to the entry of each segment it holds. A worker that reads a call packet looks the `mid` up, decodes the arguments, runs the segment natively, serializes the result and replies with one data packet. A failure inside the segment becomes an error packet whose message carries the cross-language traceback ([Error propagation](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-errors.md)). An unknown `mid` is answered with an error, never with silence. Because calls nest freely (Python calls C++, which calls back into Python), a pool must be able to serve a call while its other workers wait on another pool; [Worker model](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-workers.md) gives the rule that guarantees it.

**Function values.** A function value that crosses a cut travels as its home language, the `mid` of its manifold, and its captured values in serialized form. The receiving language wraps it in a native callable. Calling that callable sends a call packet to the home pool with the captured values followed by the new arguments, so the function always runs in the language it was built in. A suspension crosses the same way, as a callable of no arguments that runs its computation each time it is forced.

**Mutual recursion.** Morloc-defined terms are expanded at their use, so a cycle of definitions such as `isEven` and `isOdd` becomes one recursive function, rooted at the term where the cycle is entered, whose only back-edges call itself. Realization places the whole cycle in one pool ([Realization](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-realization.md)). A recursive helper defined in a `where` block is lifted into a manifold of its own, and the values it captures become extra parameters.

**Tail calls become loops.** When every back-edge of a recursive manifold is in tail position, the manifold is compiled to a loop in Python, R, C++ and Rust: its parameters become loop variables, each tail call reassigns them, and each base case returns. Tail position reaches through conditional branches, `match` arms, `let` bodies and `do` blocks. Such a recursion runs in constant stack space at any depth, even in languages that do not optimize tail calls. Three cases keep the recursion as real calls: a labeled tail call, whose hooks need a call of its own; a build with `--debug`, which keeps one frame per level for the trace; and an effectful recursion whose result is returned suspended rather than run.

**Native entries.** A recursive manifold is a pool entry, which takes and returns packets. A caller in the same pool would pay a serialization round trip on every level, quadratic in the size of a structure walked recursively. So a recursive manifold reached from its own pool gets a second, native entry that takes and returns native values, and same-pool calls use it. The serial entry keeps the original `mid` for callers in other pools and for the dispatch table. A labeled, cached or debug-traced manifold is not split, because its hooks belong to its `mid`; nor is one whose body calls another pool, unless it is a loop.

**Depth.** Recursion that is not in tail position costs one native frame per level, so it reaches the depth the same recursion written by hand reaches, less a constant. R is the exception: its generated code nests evaluation more deeply per level and reaches at least 80% of the hand-written depth. C++ and Rust pools run every call on a thread with the stack size a native main thread gets (the soft stack limit, or 8 MiB when that is unlimited), so recursion in sourced C++ or Rust also reaches its native depth. Past that depth the language’s own limit applies: Python and R raise their recursion error, and a C++ or Rust pool crashes as the native program would.


---

<!-- https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-serialization.html -->

# 13.8. Serialization

Morloc Manual > Compiler Architecture | https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-serialization.html | prev: https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-calls.md | next: https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-ownership.md

> Serialization placement runs on each pool’s tree after segmentation ([Segmentation and cross-language calls](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-calls.md)) and before ownership planning ([Ownership](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-ownership.md)). It decides where a value changes between its native form and its serialized form, and for each type and language it builds a **serialization plan**: the schema string, the native type, and the conversions a value needs at a crossing. Each pool writes the same voidstar layout for a type ([Voidstar format and schema strings](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-voidstar.md)), so two pools agree on a value with no negotiation.

**Two states.** Inside a pool, every value is either **native** (an object of the pool’s language) or **serialized** (a data packet, [Packet protocol](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-packets.md)). An argument arrives serialized; a result and an argument to a foreign call leave serialized. The pass gives every subexpression one of the two states and inserts a transition only where a use needs the other one. An argument is decoded at most once, at the entry of the function that receives it, and only if some use needs its native value. A value a pool only passes on to another pool stays a packet and is never decoded. This is also how a pool carries a value of a type it cannot hold, such as a record with no native form in a compiled language: the packet passes through unchanged.

**The plan.** For a type in a language, the plan is a tree with one node per type constructor. Each node records the wire shape (primitive, list, tuple, record, enum, variant, optional, table, stream handle, function) and the language’s native name for the constructor at that point. Three things are read off one plan, so they cannot disagree:

| Output | Use |
| --- | --- |
| Schema with hints | Given to the pool’s binding, which builds the named native container (`<dict>` in Python) while reading or writing the layout. |
| Schema without hints | Stored in packets written to disk and in the manifest. Hints never change the layout, so this form is the same in every language. |
| Native type and conversions | The type the generated code declares, and the `Packable` calls placed before writing and after reading. |

Aliases are expanded to the type they name, which gives the layout; an alias’s own native form, if it has one, supplies the hint. A built-in width such as `I64` stops the expansion, so an alias of `Int` keeps the width it names. A `data` type with no fields in any constructor is an enum; one with fields is a variant whose arms are built from the declaration, in declaration order, since the ordinal is the wire tag.

**Newtypes and `Packable`.** A newtype crosses in the form of its representation ([Naming a type: `type` and `newtype`](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/types/newtype.md)). Where the language’s native form for the newtype is the representation’s form, or a list or tuple container the binding can build directly, no conversion is needed. Otherwise the plan routes through a `Packable` instance ([Serializing custom types with `Packable`](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/types/packable.md)): the instance `Packable W N` gives `unpack :: N → W` and `pack :: W → N`, where `W` is the newtype’s representation with its parameters substituted. A sender calls `unpack` and writes `W`; a receiver reads `W` and calls `pack`. An intrinsic that acts on the value as it crosses (`@save`, `@show`, `@hash`) also unpacks first, and one that yields a value read from data (`@load`, `@read`) packs its result. A record or `data` type has a wire form of its own and never takes a `Packable` instance.

**Choosing and checking instances.** In each language the plan takes the most specific instance whose head covers the use site; two equally specific candidates are an ambiguity error, and an instance with no implementation in the language that needs it is an error naming that language. Across the program, every pair of instances whose heads can be instantiated to a common type must give it the same wire form, or the program is rejected. Because the wire form is fixed by the newtype’s declaration, the instance chosen in one language and the instance chosen in another always write and read the same layout.

**Function values.** A function crosses by defunctionalization. Every function value that may cross is a generated function with a number in its home pool, applied to zero or more captured values. Its wire form does not depend on its signature: the tuple of the home language’s name, the function number, and the captured values as self-contained packets, schema `t3sjaau1`. Captured values are embedded in their packets rather than referenced in shared memory, because the closure may be applied after the dispatch that built it has released its blocks.

![Diagram](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/static/img/mermaid-e18ddf8b613df33a589c59f164d552d7.svg)

The receiving pool **reflects** the tuple into a native callable of the right arity, using the argument and result plans the closure’s type gives. Calling it sends a call to the home pool with the captured packets followed by the new arguments. A reflected closure remembers its origin, so passing it on or back sends the original tuple, never a chain of forwarding closures. A function value can be a field of a record or an element of a list; the enclosing value’s layout carries the tuple in that slot. A suspension `<E> T` crosses the same way, as a closure of no arguments, and is never run by the crossing ([Effects](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-effects.md)). A callable that host code created has no number to call back into: it is refused where the compiler can see it and fails the call otherwise. A function or suspension has no file form, so the data-writing and data-reading intrinsics refuse types that contain one.

**Recursive types.** While building a plan the compiler keeps the set of type instantiations on the path from the root. Meeting one of them again ends the descent with a back-reference node. In the schema, the enclosing node is declared with `&` and a name, and the occurrence refers to it with `^` ([Voidstar format and schema strings](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-voidstar.md)). The key is the whole instantiation, not the name: a `Tree Int` inside a `Tree Str` is a different type and is expanded on its own. A plan whose expansion does not terminate is rejected. The layout stays finite because a variant’s payload, an optional and an array are behind pointers.

**Tables and handles.** A table’s plan is a table node listing its declared columns, written `T` or `T:` followed by the columns. The value travels as an Arrow block rather than voidstar, and the declared columns are a lower bound checked when the block is received ([Tables and tensors on the wire](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-tables.md)). A stream or file handle travels as the file’s path, and the receiving pool opens its own handle on it ([Streaming and memory mapping](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-streaming.md)).

**Strings.** Where the receiving language cannot hold a NUL byte in a string, the generated code checks received strings for one ([NUL bytes in strings](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/features/strings.md#nul-bytes)). The check is emitted only for types that contain a string, so other types pay nothing.


---

<!-- https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-ownership.html -->

# 13.9. Ownership

Morloc Manual > Compiler Architecture | https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-ownership.html | prev: https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-serialization.md | next: https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-codegen.md

> A morloc variable may be read any number of times. In generated C++ and Rust, each read must instead borrow the value, copy it, or move it. This section specifies how the compiler chooses among the three, how parameters are passed, and how the choice is checked. Ownership planning runs on each pool’s tree after serialization is placed and before code is emitted ([Code generation](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-codegen.md)). Python and R share values by reference, so they never copy and need no plan.

**An affine elaboration.** The choice translates an unrestricted source term into an affine target term: every place the source uses a value twice becomes an explicit copy, and every place it stops using one becomes an explicit release. This is the translation of intuitionistic terms into linear ones, with contraction and weakening made explicit. It preserves meaning only when copying and releasing have no observable effect. So every native type a morloc type maps to must behave as a value. A copy is independent and equal to the original. Copying, moving and releasing perform no output and touch no resource. A value holds no reference into data that something else owns, and sourced code never mutates an argument ([C++](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/languages/cpp.md), [Rust](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/languages/rust.md)). Given that, any placement that keeps the target affine is correct, and how many times a copy constructor, `Clone`, destructor or `Drop` runs is unspecified. The compiler picks a placement that copies little.

**The rules.**

| Rule | Statement |
| --- | --- |
| No use after move | Once a read moves a value, no later read on any path through the same evaluation reads it, unless a new binding of that name replaces it. A value that is never moved is released when it goes out of scope. |
| Move only at a last read | A read may move a value only if no later read on its path reads it and no other read in the same **step** does. A step is a conditional’s test, the value a body ends in, or the values one loop iteration passes to the next. Reads within a step have no order, so a value read twice in one step is moved by neither read. Reading through a local that refers into a value counts as reading that value. |
| Repeated reads never move | A read inside a lambda, a nested loop, a separate manifold or a `do` block may run any number of times, so it never moves, and no earlier read of the same value moves either. A closure that holds its own copy of each capture reads each one once, when it is built, and that read may move. |
| Loop guards borrow | A read in a condition that a loop iteration branches on, including a test of a sum type’s tag, borrows, because the chosen branch may still read the value. |
| Projection at a last read takes the field | Reading a constructor or record field at the value’s last read moves the field out and releases the rest. The value’s own destructor does not run. |
| Walking a lent value borrows | A loop-carried value borrows when it starts from a borrowed value and every iteration replaces it with a part of that value (a field, a list element, or a `match` whose arms are such parts). A borrowed structure can then be walked to any depth without copying. |

**Argument passing.** By default a native manifold takes each parameter by reference: `const T&` in C++, and `&T` in Rust for any type that is not `Copy`. Rust `Copy` types (scalars, field-free enums, and tuples and optionals of them) are passed by value. A fully applied manifold instead takes a parameter by value when its body reads that parameter once on every evaluation and **keeps** it: as the start of an owned loop value, as an element of a value it builds, or as a by-value argument to another fully applied manifold. That last case makes the decision propagate up call chains, so it is computed over the whole pool until it reaches a fixed point. The caller then moves the argument at its own last read and copies it otherwise, so a call copies at most once, and only when the caller still needs the value. A parameter kept on only one branch stays a reference, so the branch that drops it copies nothing. A closure, or any manifold that is also used as a function value, takes every parameter by reference, because one signature serves every caller.

**Planning and checking.** The plan is computed once per pool from the intermediate form, shared by both languages, and has two levels. At pool level it records which field projections take their payload and which parameters each manifold takes by value. At manifold level it records which indices hold references and which are read at more than one point. A language contributes only three facts: which of its types are free to copy, whether a tag test may read a value after a field was taken from it, and whether a list literal keeps an element without making its own copy. Rust’s own compiler rejects any read of a moved value, so a wrong Rust plan fails the build. C++ has no such check. For C++ the compiler has an independent checker that takes the plan’s decisions as given, recomputes evaluation order from the intermediate form, and reports every read that could see a taken value. Generated C++ moves at fewer positions than these rules allow, so it may make more copies than they require.


---

<!-- https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-codegen.html -->

# 13.10. Code generation

Morloc Manual > Compiler Architecture | https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-codegen.html | prev: https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-ownership.md | next: https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-interface.md

> Code generation is the last stage that works on the program’s code. It takes the per-language trees left by segmentation, serialization and ownership planning, in which every call is resolved to one implementation in one language and every crossing has a wire form, and turns each language’s share into the source text of one pool. This section specifies how pools are assembled, how user types become native definitions, which values are fixed at build time, and the properties every generated pool has whatever its language. The manifest that describes the program’s commands is built beside the pools and is specified in [Interface generation](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-interface.md).

**Input.** The unit of code generation is the **manifold**: a function the compiler generates for a call site, together with the context it needs ([Segmentation and cross-language calls](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-calls.md)). Each manifold carries an integer id, unique within the build, and a language. Manifolds are grouped by the pool they run in, which is their language’s own pool, except that a guest language’s manifolds join the pool of its host ([Language onboarding](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-onboarding.md)). Within one pool every manifold, nested ones included, is defined once under its id. Two different manifolds that would share an id in one pool are an internal compiler error, since a caller of that id would run whichever one was emitted.

**Build-time values.** Before translation, the intrinsics whose value is fixed when the program is built are replaced by literals:

| Intrinsic | Replaced by |
| --- | --- |
| `@version` | The compiler version that built the program. |
| `@compiled` | The build time, as an ISO 8601 UTC timestamp. |
| `@lang` | The name of the language whose pool evaluates it. |
| `@datafile p` | The installed location of data file `p`, or `p` unchanged when the program is not installed. |

Every other intrinsic (`@save`, `@load`, `@hash`, `@show`, the stream operations, …​) is a call into the language’s runtime binding, which implements it once for every program ([Intrinsics](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/features/intrinsics.md), [Runtime library API](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-libmorloc.md)).

**Two translators.** Every language is translated in two steps: the manifolds are lowered into one shared imperative form (statements, expressions, function definitions, and two dispatch tables), and a per-language printer writes that form as source text. The languages differ in how much of this is data:

-   A dynamically typed language (Python, R) is translated entirely from its language description: literals, list and record constructors, field and index access, function headers, lambdas, partial application, block style, and the names of the runtime calls that serialize, deserialize and call another pool are all templates in that description. No code specific to the language exists in the compiler.
-   A statically typed language (C++, Rust) has a dedicated translator, because it must render a native type for every value, emit type definitions in an order the compiler accepts, and generate marshalling code for each user type.

**Pool assembly.** Each language has a fixed pool template that holds the runtime scaffolding: process start, the arguments a pool is started with, and the hand-off to the runtime’s pool loop. The generated code is spliced into marked sections of that template:

![Diagram](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/static/img/mermaid-b8906e70d5074bf42c9be1a26858a021.svg)

| Section | Contents |
| --- | --- |
| Sources | Imports or includes of the user’s sourced files, and the language’s preamble. |
| Types | Native definitions of user types and their marshalling code (statically typed languages only). |
| Declarations | Forward declarations of every manifold, so definition order never matters. |
| Manifolds | One function per manifold, named by its id. |
| Dispatch | A local table mapping each entry point’s id to its function, and a remote table for calls that arrive as jobs from another node. |

The ids in the dispatch tables are the `mid` values the manifest records for each command, and the ids a calling pool puts in its call packets ([Packet protocol](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-packets.md)).

**Inlining keeps evaluation order.** Not every application becomes a function of its own; one that does not is written as an expression at its use. Such an inlined application is evaluated exactly where the call it replaces would have been: its statements go immediately before the statement that uses its value, in the same block. A position that is not evaluated eagerly (an arm of a conditional, the second operand of `&&` or `||`) is a block of its own, so whatever is inlined there is evaluated only if that position is.

**Native types.** A morloc type reaches a language through its native form, a template that a `type L ⇒ …​` declaration gives ([Native type mappings](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/features/foreign-functions.md#mapping-native-types)): `type Cpp ⇒ (List a) = "std::vector<$1>" a` renders `[Int]` as `std::vector<int>`, given `type Cpp ⇒ Int = "int"`. An alias with no form of its own uses its expansion’s. How user types appear in each language:

| Language | Record | `data` type with payloads |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Python | An ordered `dict` keyed by field name. | Nothing is generated; the binding builds the value from its wire form. |
| R | A named `list`. | Nothing is generated; the binding builds the value from its wire form. |
| C++ | A struct the user defines and links with `record Cpp ⇒ R = "R"`. The compiler generates its marshalling code, which reads and writes each field by its morloc name. | Generated: a struct holding a `std::variant` of `std::shared_ptr<const Arm>`, one alternative per constructor in declaration order. A type with no payloads is a generated enum. |
| Rust | A struct the user defines and links with `record Rust ⇒ R`. The compiler generates its marshalling code. | Generated, with its marshalling code. |

In C++ the declarations follow what holds what by value: enums first, then variant wrappers (which hold their arms through pointers), then records, then arm bodies, and every marshaller is declared before any is defined.

**Wrappers.** Three kinds of manifold get a wrapper around their body. A call labeled for caching looks its key up before running and stores the result after ([Caching](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/ecosystem-architecture/eco-caching.md)). A program built with `--debug` records every call in its trace ([Error propagation](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-errors.md)). A tail-recursive function that the compiler can run as a loop is emitted as one ([Segmentation and cross-language calls](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-calls.md)).

**The fingerprint.** When every pool’s source is final, the compiler hashes each one and writes the hash into the manifest. The hash covers the pool’s emitted source text, the files the program lists under `hash-include`, the build parameters, and any compiled guest objects linked into the pool, since the last two change the binary without changing the source. It is the pool’s contribution to every cache key ([Caching](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/ecosystem-architecture/eco-caching.md)), so it is computed after emission and before anything is written to disk.

**What every pool does.** Whatever its language, a generated pool:

-   is started with three trailing arguments: its socket path, the run’s temporary directory, and the shared-memory base name;
-   is ready when it answers a ping on its socket ([Process lifecycle](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-lifecycle.md));
-   answers every call with exactly one packet, a value or a failure ([Packet protocol](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-packets.md));
-   turns an error raised by user code into a failure of that call, and goes on serving;
-   is entered only through its dispatch tables, by manifold id; calls within the pool are native calls.

A language may reserve name prefixes and names for what its pool defines. A sourced name that uses one is rejected at build, so user code and generated code cannot shadow each other.

How a pool spreads its calls over threads or processes is specified in [Worker model](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-workers.md).


---

<!-- https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-interface.html -->

# 13.11. Interface generation

Morloc Manual > Compiler Architecture | https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-interface.html | prev: https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-codegen.md | next: https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-onboarding.md

> Interface generation turns the exports of a program’s main module into the command schema the manifest carries ([Compilation artifacts](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-artifacts.md)). It reads each export’s general type, its docstrings and their directives, and produces, per command, its name, its arguments with their kinds, keys, defaults and help text, its return value, and its output actions. The nexus reads nothing else, so the command line, the HTTP API and the MCP tools are all built from this one schema. This section specifies how the schema is derived and which mistakes are refused at build rather than at run time. The directives themselves are documented for users in [Docstrings](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/clis/docstrings.md), [Arguments](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/clis/arguments.md) and [Directive reference](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/clis/directive-reference.md).

**Which exports become commands.** Every term the main module exports is a subcommand, named after the term unless `@name` renames it. Its docstring’s first line is its summary, and the module’s docstring describes the program. `--* group:` lines in the export list put the exports that follow into a named group of subcommands. Three kinds of export are treated specially:

| Export | Treatment |
| --- | --- |
| Generic: its type still has a type variable | Not a command. The build warns, naming it, and builds the others. |
| A function in an argument or the result, or a suspension below the root of one | Rejected at build, naming the position: a command’s arguments and result are data, and a function has no data form. |
| A suspension at the root of an argument or the result | Adapted at the boundary: the command builds the suspension from the caller’s value, or runs it for the caller. |

**Remote and pure commands.** A command whose body calls a foreign function is **remote**: the schema records the id of its entry manifold, the pool that holds it, and every pool the command can reach, so a one-shot run starts only those. A command that calls no foreign function is **pure**: the schema holds the expression itself, in a small language of literals, applications of built-in operations and intrinsics, and the command’s arguments, and the nexus evaluates it without starting a pool ([Runtime overview](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-overview.md)). Build-time intrinsics in a pure command are fixed as they are in pools ([Code generation](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-codegen.md)).

**From docstring to argument.** Each argument’s docstring is the nearest one: written on the type in the signature, else on the type alias named there, else on the next alias down its chain. A term never inherits another term’s docstring by assignment. The directives then decide the argument’s kind:

| Kind | Made by | Rules checked at build |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Positional | the default | Takes no `@default`. An optional (`?T`) positional may be left off, so every positional after one must be optional too. |
| Option | `@arg` | Requires a `@default`, except under `@many` (default `[]`) and for a literal `?Str` (default null). |
| Flag | `@true` or `@false` on a `Bool` argument | `@true` turns a false default on, `@false` turns a true default off; `@arg` is refused. A `Bool` with neither is a positional. |
| Record group | `@unroll` on a record | Each field becomes its own option or flag, with its own docstring. |
| Constructor choice | `@unroll` on a `data` type | One option per constructor; exactly one is given, unless the type is optional or has a default. |

Further rules hold across a command’s arguments: at most one positional takes `@many`, and it is the last positional; at most one reads standard input, and it is the last positional; `@stdin`, `@many`, `@default` and `@unroll` reject the combinations that would give one slot two shapes. Each argument’s shape directives (`source`, `form`, `check.path`) are checked against its wire type ([Input shape](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/clis/input-shape.md)), and a default is parsed and checked against the argument’s type, so a wrong default is a build error rather than a run-time one.

**Keys.** Every argument is given one **key**, published in the schema, that every interface other than the command line uses to name it: an option or flag by its long spelling (else its short one), a positional by its `@name` or else by *and its 1-based place among the positionals, a field of an unrolled record by its field name. The compiler computes the key once, so no interface derives its own, and it rejects two arguments of one command that would publish the same key. Keys beginning with* are reserved for generated names and for `_render`, the output selector.

**Two schemas per value.** Each argument and the return value carry two schema strings ([Voidstar format and schema strings](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-voidstar.md)). The **concrete** schema includes the hints of the language that will receive the value, and is what the nexus encodes the call with. The **general** schema has those hints removed, and is what the machine-readable help publishes, so the published contract does not change when a function moves to another language.

**Output actions.** Each `@with` or `@render` directive ([Output actions](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/clis/output-actions.md)) becomes an action of its command, recorded with its flag, its handler’s summary, whether it writes raw bytes (`@render`) or a typed value (`@with`), and whether it is the `@default`; a second `@default` is a build error. For each action the compiler also builds hidden commands: one that runs the parent and applies the handler to the fresh result, and one that applies the handler to output the parent saved earlier. The latter is omitted, with the reason recorded, when the action cannot run on saved output. Each action is classed by how it consumes the parent’s output: a whole value, a gathered stream, a stream processed batch by batch, or a fold. A streaming command also records the type of its batches, since its return type is `()`. An argument read through `@parse` gets a hidden entry command of its own that applies the parse functions before the call.

![Diagram](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/static/img/mermaid-57669d06addeddd2d33c405e38bdfdd6.svg)

**One schema, every interface.** The command-line parser, the three help tiers, `--json-help` ([The interface as data](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/clis/interface-as-data.md)), the daemon’s API and the MCP tool list are all built by the nexus from the command schema ([Serving](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/ecosystem-architecture/eco-serving.md)). The command line reads each argument from its text form using the shape directives; every other interface takes the argument’s JSON value under its key. An argument left out takes the default the schema gives it on every interface.


---

<!-- https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-onboarding.html -->

# 13.12. Language onboarding

Morloc Manual > Compiler Architecture | https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-onboarding.html | prev: https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-interface.md | next: https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-libmorloc.md

> A language joins Morloc through four things: a **language description** that the compiler reads as data, a code generator that writes its pools, a **binding** to the runtime library that its pools call, and a library module that maps Morloc’s base types and functions into it. This section specifies what each must provide, how a guest language that has no pool of its own is attached to a host, and the behavior that makes a binding conforming. It is the checklist for adding a language; the pieces it names are specified in the sections it links to.

**The language description.** Everything the compiler needs to know about a language that is not code generation is declared as data, not built into the compiler:

| Declaration | Used for |
| --- | --- |
| Name, aliases, file extension | Resolving `source Py from …​` and `type Py ⇒ …​` to the language, and naming its files. |
| Compiled or interpreted, and the run command | Whether the pool is built into a binary or run as a script by an interpreter. The manifest’s start command for the pool is derived from these ([Compilation artifacts](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-artifacts.md)). |
| Name and operator patterns | Which sourced names are legal. A sourced name that matches neither, such as a fragment of code, is rejected at build. |
| Reserved prefixes and names | Names the pool defines for itself. A sourced name that uses one is rejected at build. |
| Whether a `Str` may hold a NUL byte | A language that cannot carry one has such strings refused at the boundary into its pool. |
| Preamble | Lines placed at the top of every pool, with the Morloc home and library directories filled in. |
| Call costs | The cost of a call within the language, of a call into it from another language, and of any pair of languages that bypasses the usual crossing. Realization weighs implementations with these ([Realization](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-realization.md)). |
| Host | For a guest language only: the language whose pool it runs in. |
| Dependencies | The runtime and the packages a pool needs, each marked as needed to build, to run, or both, and optionally as needed only by some programs. The environment manager installs them ([Environments](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/ecosystem-architecture/eco-environments.md)). |

**The code generator.** A dynamically typed language is generated entirely from templates in its description: literals (including infinities and NaN), list, tuple and record constructors, index and field access, assignment, function headers and block style, lambdas, partial application, the import statement for a sourced file, the entries of the two dispatch tables, and the names of the binding’s functions that serialize, deserialize and call another pool. A statically typed language needs a translator of its own, because it must render a native type for every value and generate type definitions and marshalling code ([Code generation](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-codegen.md)). Either kind also supplies a pool template: the fixed scaffolding into which the generated sections are spliced.

**Build parameters.** A compiled language’s builder reads its own keys from the `-X LANG:KEY=VALUE` parameters ([Build parameters](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/languages/build-parameters.md)) and validates their values itself; the compiler stores them without interpreting them. The key `flags` is reserved in every language as a raw, ordered passthrough to the compile command.

**The binding.** A pool talks to the rest of the program only through the runtime library ([Runtime library API](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/compiler-architecture/compiler-libmorloc.md)). The binding exposes it to the language: an extension module for an interpreted language, a library that a compiled pool links. It must provide:

-   conversion between the language’s native values and the binary form, in both directions, driven by the value’s schema ([Voidstar format and schema strings](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-voidstar.md));
-   reading and writing packets, and the shared-memory references they carry ([Packet protocol](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-packets.md), [Shared memory layout](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-shm.md));
-   the foreign call, which sends a call packet to another pool and returns its result or raises its failure in the caller;
-   the runtime intrinsics, such as `@save`, `@load`, `@hash` and the stream operations;
-   the pool loop. A threaded pool hands its two dispatch tables to the runtime’s pool main loop. A forking pool hands the runtime’s scheduler a callback that runs one job; the scheduler binds the socket and forks, retires and replaces workers ([Worker model](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/build-architecture/build-workers.md)).

**The base library.** Morloc’s base types have no meaning in a language until a module gives them native forms (`type Py ⇒ Int = "int"`, `type Cpp ⇒ (List a) = "std::vector<$1>" a`), and the base functions until it sources implementations of them. Each shipped language has such a module, named `root-` and the language (`root-py`, `root-cpp`).

**Guest languages.** A guest has no pool. Its sourced functions are compiled into its host’s pool and called there, so a call between guest and host is a native call, not a crossing. Before realization, the compiler builds each guest source file into a linkable library with the guest’s own compiler, checks each sourced Morloc signature against the entry point the guest compiler reports (arity, element types and rank), generates host glue that converts the host’s native values to the guest’s and back, and rewrites each guest source into an ordinary host source that calls the glue. From then on the guest is invisible: the host pool links its objects, and those objects are folded into the pool’s fingerprint ([Caching](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/ecosystem-architecture/eco-caching.md)). A guest signature may use only types the guest can represent. Futhark is a guest of C++ ([Futhark](https://morloc-project.github.io/docs/languages/futhark.md)), restricted to fixed-width numeric scalars and vectors and matrices of them.

**Conformance.** A binding is conforming when every program means the same thing whichever language the compiler picks for a call. Concretely:

| Behavior | Requirement |
| --- | --- |
| Crossing | A value sent to another language and back arrives equal to the original, whatever the route (inline, shared memory, file). |
| `Int` | Arrives as the language’s own default integer type. Fixed-width types keep their width. |
| Functions | A function value crosses as a native callable that runs in the language where it was built, called with each argument group as the source signature writes it. |
